profiles.label: Lancia Delta HF Integrale Evoluzione II (Evo 2)
profiles.framing: This is the final, catalyzed 215hp development of the homologation-bred Integrale, and at current money it is a blue-chip Group A icon that the buyer intends to actually drive on Carmel Valley Road and Highway 1 — not park in a bubble. For this buyer the car must be a documented, unmolested, rust-free, numbers-correct Evo 2 with a legible ownership chain from Europe through import, because originality and provenance carry most of the value and almost all of the resale risk. Mechanically it is a hand-built Fiat-group turbo four with a demanding service clock: it rewards a fastidious owner and punishes deferred maintenance brutally. The decision hinges far more on rust, authenticity paperwork, and service history than on odometer reading.
profiles.weak_points: ['Structural and cosmetic rust is the number one killer. Check the front strut towers and inner fender seams, the sills at the jacking points, the floor pans under the front carpets (water gets in past the plenum/scuttle drains and the windshield seal), the rear inner arches behind the boxed Evo fender flares, the tailgate lower edge and around the rear wiper motor, the sunroof drain channels if fitted, and the fuel filler bowl. Cars that lived in Northern Europe or spent winters in Italy are commonly patched. Proper metalwork plus a color-matched respray on a Blue Lagos car runs $8,000–30,000 and permanently dents value; look for old bodyshop invoices, paint-depth-gauge readings and photos of the car on a lift with the arch liners out.', 'Cambelt service is time-based, not mileage-based. The interval is roughly every 3 years or 36,000 km, and a snapped belt on this interference 16V head means bent valves and a $6,000–12,000 head rebuild. A 2020 belt on a 2026 car is out of date regardless of the 41,000 km on the clock. Demand a dated invoice covering belt, tensioner, water pump, and ideally the balance-shaft/auxiliary belt, from a shop that knows Lancias.', 'Head gasket failure and warped/cracked cylinder heads are classic Integrale problems, aggravated by overboost, poor coolant maintenance, and cars that sit. Symptoms: coolant loss with no external leak, pressurized expansion tank, mayonnaise under the cam cover, hot-idle misfire. Budget $4,000–8,000 for head off, skim, gasket, and valve work; a full bottom-end rebuild with pistons and rods is $18,000–30,000 at a specialist.', 'Turbo and boost control. The Garrett T3 (water-cooled) suffers shaft play and seal failure from hot shutdowns and stale oil; the wastegate actuator, boost solenoid and the vacuum/boost hose spaghetti perish and cause overboost cuts or soft running. Evo 2 cars also crack the cast exhaust manifold between runners. Turbo rebuild/replacement $2,000–4,500; manifold $1,200–2,500 with labor; hose renewal kit plus tuning $800–1,500.', 'Driveline: the Ferguson viscous center coupling degrades with age and low use, and a seized or dead VC gives tight-turn binding, driveline wind-up or vague traction; the Torsen rear diff can whine and its output seals leak. The five-speed transaxle is weak on second-gear synchro and suffers a notchy/obstructive shift from worn linkage bushings and a tired clutch hydraulic system. VC $2,000–3,500 installed, gearbox rebuild $4,500–8,000, clutch (dual-mass-free but labor-heavy) $1,800–3,000.', 'Cooling system and hot-running. Radiator, intercooler-to-throttle plumbing, the header/expansion tank and its cap, and the electric fan switch are all failure-prone; these cars run hot in traffic and a late fan is how heads get warped. Plan on a new radiator, hoses, thermostat, cap and fan relay as a matter of course — $1,500–2,500.', 'Bosch ABS system (ATE/Bosch hydraulic unit, accumulator and pump). A pulsing or permanently lit ABS light usually means a dead accumulator or pump motor; parts are scarce, and a rebuilt unit is $1,500–3,500. Test brake pedal feel and warning-light behavior cold and after a drive.', 'Electrics and grounds. Corroded earth points behind the battery tray and in the footwells cause phantom faults: dash warning lights, power window failure, erratic fuel gauge, fan and fuel-pump relay dropouts. The Marelli/Weber IAW ECU is generally robust but the crank sensor, air-temp sensor and injector harness insulation age out. Body ECU/relay board issues and the 5-digit odometer make mileage verification a documentation exercise, not an instrument-cluster one.', 'Interior trim is fragile and largely NLA. Dash tops crack, the Recaro bolsters and Crème leather on Blue Lagos cars stain and split, the center-dash oil pressure/temp gauge pod fades, headliners droop, and Evo-specific items (hood vents, adjustable rear spoiler, flare trim, Speedline Montecarlo center caps, correct Momo wheel) are expensive or unobtainable. Faded or
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Fresh timing belt, tensioner, water pump and auxiliary belts regardless of the last invoice date if it is over ~3 years old ($1,500–2,800)', 'Four new tires in correct 205/45ZR16 fitment plus alignment and corner-weight-sane setup ($1,400–2,200)', 'Full fluid service: engine oil, gearbox/transaxle, rear diff, coolant flush, brake and clutch fluid ($600–1,200)', 'Brake system refresh — flex lines, pads, bleed, and rotor inspection; ABS accumulator function test ($900–2,500)', 'Replace all vacuum/boost hoses and check boost solenoid and wastegate operation; road-tune to spec boost ($600–1,500)', 'Battery, grounds cleanup, and relay/fuse box inspection; fix any dash warning lights ($300–900)', 'Fuel filter, and on a low-use car an in-tank pump and hose inspection plus injector cleaning ($40
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch and hydraulics if the pedal is high or the shift is obstructive ($1,800–3,000)', 'Viscous center coupling replacement if any wind-up or binding appears ($2,000–3,500)', 'Radiator, thermostat, header tank and fan switch renewal ($1,200–2,500)', 'Turbo rebuild or replacement and exhaust manifold inspection/replacement ($2,000–4,500)', 'A/C system rebuild or conversion ($1,500–3,000)', 'Suspension bushings, engine/gearbox mounts, dampers and top mounts ($2,000–4,000)', 'Cosmetic sorting: seat bolster repair, dash pod or gauge refurbishment, center-cap and trim replacement ($1,000–4,000)', 'Localized rust remediation and paint blending if any bubbling is found at the arches or sills ($2,500–10,000)']
profiles.market_notes: Evo 2 sits at the top of the Integrale ladder, and within it the special editions — Blue Lagos, Giallo Ginestra, Bianco Perlato, Dealers Collection, Club HF Collection — carry a large premium over standard Rosso/Nero cars, with documented low-km, single-repaint-free examples now trading well into six figures. Provenance is price: a Lancia registry entry, original libretto/Fahrzeugbrief, matching engine and chassis numbers, an unbroken service file with dated cambelt invoices, and clean import paperwork can be worth 20–40% versus an undocumented car. Rust history, a respray, replaced Evo-specific trim, or a converted lesser Integrale destroy value disproportionately; conversely high-km but immaculate, heavily documented driver cars trade at a steep discount to museum-km cars and are often the better buy for someone who will actually use it. Manual is the only transmission; RHD conversions and non-original turbo/ECU tuning are discounts.
profiles.catchup_notes: Even a 26k-mile Evo 2 is a 30-plus-year-old Italian turbo car whose rubber, fluids and fuel system have aged on the calendar rather than the odometer, so assume a full recommissioning: cambelt package, all coolant/vacuum/fuel hoses, tires, brake and clutch hydraulics, fluids, and battery/grounds. Low-mileage cars that sat are often worse than driven ones for seals, tank varnish, seized calipers and flat-spotted bushings. Budget roughly $6,000–10,000 of catch-up in the first year on a well-kept example, more if the A/C, ABS accumulator or viscous coupling need attention.

profiles.label: Land Rover LR4 / Discovery 4 (L319, 2010–2016, incl. HSE Lux & Landmark)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the LR4 is a genuinely capable, seven-seat family and Central Coast adventure wagon: Terrain Response, twin-speed transfer case, air suspension and real ground clearance in a package that still rides like a luxury car on Highway 1. It is not an investment and should never be bought as one — final-year 2016 Landmark cars have a modest collector halo, but running costs behave like a used luxury SUV with a hand-built British electrical system. What matters is documentation of the expensive stuff (timing chain hardware on the AJ126 supercharged V6, coolant pipes, air suspension, differentials) and a car that has been serviced by a specialist rather than deferred. Buy the best-documented example, not the cheapest, and budget a real reserve from day one.
profiles.weak_points:
1) AJ126 3.0 supercharged V6 timing chain and tensioner wear (2014–2016 cars, and the related AJ133 5.0 V8 chain issue on 2010–2013): a cold-start rattle of 1–3 seconds, chain stretch codes (P0016/P0017/P0018), or a whirring/ticking at idle points to guides and hydraulic tensioners. Failure is catastrophic (valve-to-piston contact). Preventive chain service is engine-out or front-cover-off labor, roughly $6,000–$10,000 at an independent, more at a dealer. Ask for a cold-start video with sound and any chain/tensioner invoices; unrecorded 90k+ cars carry this risk unpriced.
2) Plastic coolant crossover pipes / thermostat housing / water pump on the 3.0 SC: the OEM composite pipes under the supercharger go brittle with heat cycles and can split without warning, dumping coolant and risking overheat damage to an aluminum engine. Aftermarket billet-aluminum pipe upgrade kits exist and are the tell of a knowledgeable owner; expect $1,200–$2,500 done with the water pump and thermostat while access is open. Look for a receipt naming 'coolant crossover pipes,' 'aluminum pipe upgrade,' or supercharger removal.
3) Supercharger nose-cone bearings and the isolator/coupler: a whine changing pitch or a rattle at idle around 80–120k miles. Nose cone rebuild $600–$1,200; whole blower far more.
4) Air suspension: EAS compressor (Hitachi/AMK) and dryer wear out around 80–130k miles, symptoms are slow rise, 'Suspension Fault' messages, a car that sits low overnight, or a compressor that runs long and hot. Compressor with dryer $600–$1,400 installed; individual air springs $350–$700 each; valve block and height sensors add up. Coil-spring conversions are a red flag on a car this buyer wants unmodified.
5) Cooling-system periphery generally: expansion tank cracks, radiator and intercooler-circuit auxiliary pump, and the low-temp radiator on SC cars. A one-time overheat event can cook the engine — check for coolant staining in the vee and Carfax/dealer notes of 'overheating.'
6) Rear differential and driveshaft: rear diff bearing whine and pinion seal leaks appear from ~90k; center support bearing and rear driveshaft U-joints/flex disc cause a 40–60 mph vibration or clunk on throttle transitions. Driveshaft $700–$1,400, rear diff rebuild/replace $1,800–$3,500.
7) Front suspension wear items: lower control arm bushings and ball joints, plus front upper arms — typical at 70–110k, causing a shimmy over the mid-corner ruts on local backroads. All four arms $1,200–$2,000; alignment mandatory after air-suspension or arm work.
8) Sunroof and body drains: the triple-sunroof cars (Landmark, HSE Lux) plug drains and wet the headliner, A-pillars and, worse, the passenger footwell and front SRS/BCM connectors — check for damp carpet padding and musty smell. Also alpine window seals and tailgate/upper-glass hinge corrosion.
9) Electrical gremlins and parasitic drain: a weak battery causes cascading warning lights (park brake, suspension, transmission fault). Electric parking brake actuator module failure ($700–$1,200), HVAC blend-door actuators, front and rear camera/infotainment modules, and door-latch/window regulator faults are common. Always test every module cold and hot.
10) In-tank fuel pump / low-pressure fuel supply failures on the SC V6 (this generation has documented pump replacements around 60–90k, ~$900–$1,600) plus high-pressure pump and injector issues showing as long crank or misfire under load.
11) Oil leaks: cam cover gaskets, oil cooler/filter housing, and the timing cover on high-mile motors — usually $500–$1,500 each depending on access; a soaked engine bay masks the more serious coolant leaks.
12) Transmission: the ZF 8HP is strong but was 'filled for life.' A 98k car with no fluid service should get a pan/filter/fluid change ($500–$800); look for shudder at light throttle 1,200–1,600 rpm (torque converter lock-up) and harsh 2-3 shifts.
13) Brakes and tires: heavy vehicle, front rotors/pads every 30–40k ($900–$1,400 axle set with rotors); 20
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up (engine oil, ZF 8HP pan/filter/fluid if undocumented, front/rear diff and transfer case fluid, brake fluid, coolant condition test); four matching tires if the set is mixed or aged; new AGM battery unless dated within ~3 years; air-suspension full-cycle test and likely compressor/dryer service; clear all stored fault codes and re-scan after a 100-mile shakedown; clean all four sunroof and A-pillar drains; front brake pads/rotors if under 4mm; correct any cam-cover or oil-cooler seepage. Expect $2,500–$5,000 on a typical 90–100k example.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Coolant crossover pipe upgrade with water pump and thermostat if not already documented ($1,200–$2,500); front lower control arm bushings/ball joints and alignment ($1,200–$2,000); air spring(s) or valve block as leaks appear ($400–$1,500); supercharger nose-cone bearing or isolator if whining ($600–$1,200); rear driveshaft center bearing/flex disc or rear diff seals ($700–$1,800); HVAC actuator, parking-brake module or camera/infotainment module repair ($400–$1,200); spark plugs and both drive belts if not stamped. Timing-chain service is the big contingency if any cold-start rattle or chain codes appear.
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by service documentation — a folder showing coolant pipes, chain hardware, air suspension and transmission service is worth several thousand dollars over an equal-mileage mystery car. Final-year 2016 cars, especially the Landmark and HSE Lux with three sunroofs, Meridian, surround cameras and the HD/heavy-duty package (full-size matching spare, locking rear diff), carry a premium; missing HD pack and mismatched 20" tires are cheapening details. Sub-80k-mile examples and desirable color combos (Santorini Black, Fuji White, Corris Grey over Ebony) bring the strongest money, while any Carfax damage entries, unrepaired suspension faults, or coil-spring conversions produce steep discounts. Regional bidding for these on BaT clusters $18k–$32k depending on miles and records, with hollow-market risk below $15k where the buyer inherits every deferred item.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 90–100k mile LR4 arrives with life-of-vehicle fluids never changed, an aging battery causing phantom faults, a tired air-suspension compressor and original coolant pipes. Plan on a comprehensive fluid and consumables catch-up plus air-suspension and cooling-system attention in the first year, and treat undocumented timing-chain hardware as an open $6k–$10k liability rather than a solved problem.

profiles.label: Lexus LX 470 (J100, 1998–2007)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the LX 470 is the long-haul family/adventure truck: a 100-Series Land Cruiser with a bulletproof 2UZ-FE V8, full-time 4WD with a locking center diff, and enough leather and sound deadening to make Highway 1 and I-5 runs painless. Bought right, it is a 300k-mile vehicle; bought wrong, it is a rusty AHC-warning-light money pit with a $1,500 starter job hiding under the intake. What matters most here is a documented maintenance trail (timing belt/water pump, fluids, front axle service), a genuinely clean underbody, and an honest answer on the hydraulic suspension — either working and serviced, or converted with receipts and quality parts. Coastal Carmel salt air makes a rust-free California/Southwest history worth real money over a Northeast truck with a 'protected' frame.
profiles.weak_points: 1) AHC/TEMS hydraulic suspension is the defining risk. The nitrogen accumulators ('globes') lose charge by 100–150k miles, giving a harsh ride, slow raise/lower, and eventually an AHC warning light; globes run ~$150–250 each (four) plus labor, height control cylinders, the pump/accumulator assembly, and the height sensors add up fast — a full factory refresh is commonly $2,500–4,500. AHC fluid should be flushed every ~60k with Toyota AHC fluid; look for flush receipts and for the truck to cycle Low→N→High smoothly with pressure readings within spec (Techstream). Many trucks, like the example, have been 'AHC deleted' to conventional coils/shocks (OME, Dobinsons, Slee brackets) — that is an accepted and often preferable fix, but demand parts receipts, correct front spring rate, proper rear conversion hardware, and confirmation the dash lights/controls were addressed; a cheap delete with worn-out donor springs rides badly and sags. 2) Timing belt on the 2UZ-FE is due every 90k miles/9 years — always replaced with water pump, idler/tensioner bearings, thermostat, cam/crank seals and drive belts; $900–1,600 at an independent. A 2006 with a 2022/92k belt is on the clock by date, not miles, so budget it again around 2031 or sooner. 3) Starter is buried under the intake manifold: the part is ~$300 but labor makes it a $1,200–1,900 job; slow/clicking cranks or a hot-start hesitation means plan it, and do the intake-area hoses, PCV, and knock sensors while it is open. 4) Front axle service is the classic neglected item — birfield/CV joints, inner axle seals, knuckle wiper seals and wheel bearing repack; symptoms are grease slung on the inside of the wheels, gear-oil weeping from the knuckle, or a clicking on full-lock turns; a proper both-sides knuckle rebuild is $1,200–2,200. 5) Steering: power steering pump and high-pressure hose leaks, and on AHC trucks the pump also feeds the suspension, so a weeping pump is a two-system problem; sector shaft/box play and worn idler arm bushing cause the wandering 'Land Cruiser vagueness' — box, idler arm, and drag link/tie rod ends together are $1,000–2,000. 6) Suspension bushings and lower ball joints: original ball joints at 150k+ are a genuine safety item (use Toyota/555, not cheap aftermarket); upper/lower control arm bushings and sway bar bushings clunk from 120k. 7) Rust: rear frame section above the spring perches/rear crossmember, frame rails near the leaf-less coil mounts, rear quarter inner arches, hatch lower edge and tailgate seam, brake and fuel lines, and the rear bumper mounts — Northeast/Midwest trucks need the frame probed with a pick, not just photographed; a 'Woolwax/Fluid Film applied' note is good hygiene but can also mask scale. 8) Cooling and leaks: original radiator end tanks crack and the OEM radiator seeps at 120–180k ($500–800 installed); valve cover gaskets, oil cooler lines, front and rear main seals, and the oil pan (RTV, not gasket) commonly weep by 150k. 9) HVAC: rear heater lines corrode, blend-door/servo actuators fail causing one-side-cold, and the heater core is a dash-out job ($1,200–2,000); check both front and rear A/C blow cold and that the rear unit actually works. 10) Electronics: Mark Levinson amplifier and the 6-disc changer fail, the factory nav/display screen pixelates or goes dark, and the aging head unit is a $600–1,500 problem to solve properly (many owners fit a modern unit, which affects the 'unmodified' box but not the truck's integrity). 11) Interior wear items: sagging headliner, cracked dash top on sun-belt trucks, driver seat bolster and steering wheel leather wear, power antenna failures, and third-row latch/strap breakage; also door-lock actuators and the sliding-glass moonroof drains. 12) Driveline: rear driveshaft double-cardan and slip yoke wear causing vibration at 45–65 mph, propeller shaft flange bolt fretting (Toyota TSB), and differential/transfer case breather hoses; ATF (A343F on pre-'05, A750F on '05–'07) should have drain-and-fil
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid reset: engine oil, transfer case, front/rear differentials, transmission drain-and-fill, brake fluid, coolant if not pink/recent, and AHC fluid flush if still hydraulic. Replace the battery and terminals if age unknown, all four wipers, cabin/engine air filters, serpentine belt if undated. Expect a front-end refresh: lower ball joints, idler arm bushing, tie rod ends and an alignment if steering is vague ($800–1,600). Tires are commonly date-expired even with tread left — budget $1,000–1,400 for a set of 275/65R18 all-terrains. Fix any active AHC/VSC light, and address the usual minor leaks (valve covers, oil pan RTV weep) plus a rear main inspection. On a Northeast truck: dry-ice or needle-gun the frame, neutralize, prime, and re-cavity-wax before the first coastal winter ($800
profiles.repairs_12mo: Timing belt/water pump service if the current one is over ~7 years old regardless of mileage ($900–1,600). Starter replacement done proactively with intake off if cranking is at all lazy ($1,200–1,900). Front axle knuckle rebuild with birfields, inner seals and bearing repack if grease slinging or knuckle weeping ($1,200–2,200). Radiator and upper/lower hoses if original. AHC globes (all four) plus pump/height sensor attention if the truck is still hydraulic and rides harshly ($1,500–3,000), or a proper coil conversion with quality springs/shocks if going that route ($2,000–3,500 installed). Rear driveshaft double-cardan rebuild or replacement for highway vibration, control arm and sway bar bushings, blower/blend actuator work, headliner re-stretch, and a decent audio/nav solution if the M
profiles.market_notes: The 2003–2007 facelift trucks carry a clear premium, and 2005–2007 most of all for the VVT-i 4.7, 5-speed automatic, and updated interior/nav; a clean 2006 with sub-100k miles, two owners, and full records is the top of the market. Documented service (timing belt with water pump, AHC flushes or a receipted quality conversion, front axle service) moves price more than cosmetics, and a genuinely rust-free Western truck is worth $3,000–6,000 over an equivalent-mile salt-belt example. AHC that works and has been maintained appeals to purists; a well-executed delete is neutral-to-positive for most buyers and removes the biggest liability, while a broken AHC with lights on knocks thousands off. Third row, Mark Levinson, and locking center diff are expected on later trucks; conservative colors, tan/ivory interiors in good shape, and stock 18s help, while lifts, big tires, and bumpers narrow the buyer pool.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any J100 as 18–28 years old first and low-mileage second: rubber, hoses, belts, bushings, tires, and the AHC/power steering fluid circuits age out on the calendar even at 97k miles. A typical honest example needs $3,000–6,000 of deferred catch-up in the first year — fluids everywhere, front-end wear parts, a timing belt reset by date, cooling system refresh, and frame/underbody cleanup and cavity waxing if it spent time in the salt belt.

profiles.label: Lexus RX 350 (AL10, 3rd generation)
profiles.framing: This is the low-drama family/utility slot in the garage: a 2GR-powered, port-or-D4S V6 crossover with a properly engineered automatic, a quiet cabin, and a parts and service network that reaches everywhere. For a Carmel-based buyer it is a Highway 1 / Salinas run-around and airport hauler that should never be the reason a weekend gets cancelled. Nothing about it is engaging, so the entire buying case rests on documentation, condition, and price relative to a market that stubbornly refuses to depreciate. Note that US-market 2010–2015 cars are the true AL10 with the 2GR-FE and U660E/U760E; 2016 is the AL20 redesign with the 2GR-FKS and 8-speed — mechanically similar in spirit but a different platform, so verify which car you are actually looking at.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing-cover and cam-tower oil seepage on the 2GR-FE is the signature 100k+ issue: the RTV-sealed front cover weeps down the back of the block and onto the subframe, often mistaken for a rear main leak. Diagnosis is easy from below with a light; repair is engine-out-of-the-way labor at roughly $1,800–3,000 at an independent. Ask for photos of a clean underside or a documented reseal. 2) Water pump failure/weeping around 80k–130k, usually announced by pink crust at the weep hole or a faint coolant smell; $500–900 including the belt. 3) The VVT-i oil supply line failure that killed early 2GR engines was addressed by recall/updated hard line on earlier cars, but on any 2GR verify the metal line is present and dry — a burst line dumps oil in seconds and destroys the engine. 4) U660E/U760E 6-speed: Lexus calls the WS fluid 'lifetime,' which it is not. Neglected units develop a 1-2 shift flare, torque-converter shudder at light throttle 35–50 mph, or a delayed engagement clunk. Drain-and-fills every 60k are cheap insurance; a car at 120k with zero fluid history is a $3,500–5,000 gamble. 2013+ F Sport uses the 8-speed U880E, which is fine but has its own valve-body software updates. 5) Melting/sticky and cracking dashboards on 2010–2013 cars, especially sun-belt and coastal-sun examples — Lexus ran a warranty extension that has now expired; replacement is $1,400–2,500. Check the top pad and the passenger airbag seam. 6) HVAC blend-door and mode actuators tick or knock behind the dash and cause split hot/cold; $250–600 each depending on access. 7) Remote Touch mouse controller and the 8-inch nav screen: sticky/erratic cursor, ghost touches, screen delamination or DVD/HDD nav drive failure. New OEM units are $900–1,800; many owners live with it or fit an aftermarket head unit (a modification this buyer should be wary of, as it often means hacked wiring). 8) Power liftgate struts and the electric lift actuator/motor fail around 100k — the gate drops, beeps, or refuses to latch; struts are cheap, the actuator is $600–1,000. 9) Suspension: front lower control arm bushings, sway bar end links, and strut mounts produce a clunk over Carmel Valley pavement joints by 100k–120k; struts and mounts all around run $1,200–2,000. Rear wheel bearings hum from ~120k, $400–600 each. 10) Hydraulic engine and transmission mounts collapse and cause a diesel-like idle shake in Drive; front mount $350–650 installed. 11) Spark plugs are a 120k service and the rear bank requires intake plenum removal — budget $450–700, not $120. 12) A/C condenser stone damage and slow leaks are common on freeway cars; condenser plus recharge $700–1,100. Also check for the compressor clutch rattle at idle. 13) AWD models: the transfer case and rear diff fluids are almost never changed, and the driveshaft center support bearing rumbles at 40–60 mph on higher-mileage cars. 14) Sunroof drains clog with coastal pine needles and Monterey litter, soaking the A-pillar trim and headliner — pull the trim and look for water staining, plus check the spare well for standing water.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up: transmission WS drain-and-fill (repeat in 500 miles if the old fluid is dark), coolant if past 10 years, brake fluid flush, transfer case and rear diff on AWD. Four new tires if the DOT codes are over six years old regardless of tread (very common on low-mile Lexus SUVs), plus an alignment. New 12V battery if undated or over four years, cabin and engine air filters, wiper blades, and a sunroof-drain flush. Expect to fix at least one HVAC actuator tick or a pair of liftgate struts. Budget $1,500–2,800.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if not documented; timing-cover reseal if seepage is dripping rather than weeping; spark plugs and coil inspection at 120k; front strut assemblies and sway bar links if it clunks; engine and transmission mounts if it shakes at idle in Drive; a rear wheel bearing; brake pads and rotors all around; possibly a dash pad replacement on a 2010–2013 sun-baked car. Budget $2,000–4,000.
profiles.market_notes: RX 350s trade on records and mileage bands more than on spec — a one-owner car with a full Lexus dealer history and under 90k will command a real premium over an identical 120k trade-in. AWD carries a modest premium nationally but matters little on the Monterey Peninsula, so FWD is the value play; Navigation/Premium/Luxury packages, ventilated seats, blind-spot monitor, and the 2013+ F Sport add appeal, while the F Sport's stiffer ride and 19s add nothing for this mission. Neutral colors (Nebula Gray, Starfire Pearl, silver) with tan or black leather sell fastest; a clean, unmodified California car with no rust, no accidents, and a factory head unit is worth paying up for because the whole point of this vehicle is not thinking about it.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-15 year old RX arrives with 'lifetime' fluids that were never changed, original coolant, aging suspension bushings, and six-to-eight-year-old tires on a low-mile example. Plan on a full fluids-and-rubber reset in the first month — trans, coolant, brake fluid, diff/transfer case, tires, battery, belt — then treat water pump, spark plugs, and struts as scheduled 12-month items rather than surprises.

profiles.label: Mazda MX-5 Miata (NA, 1990–1997)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the NA Miata is a cheap-to-own, top-down Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road car — a 2,200-lb, 116–133 hp roadster whose whole appeal is steering feel, shifter quality and the ability to drive it hard at legal-ish speeds. It is not a hauler and not an investment; the right car is a rust-free, documented, largely stock West Coast example where the timing belt, cooling system and soft top are already sorted. Because purchase price is low relative to the cost of fixing a bad one, condition and documentation matter far more than mileage or a rare color. A tidy 80k-mile car with receipts beats a 45k-mile survivor with an unknown belt history every time.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt: the 1.6L (B6ZE) and 1.8L (BP) are interference-risk on the 1.8 and generally considered non-interference on the 1.6, but either way the belt, tensioner, water pump and front seals are a 60k-mile/7-year item. Most NAs on the market are overdue. Expect $600–$1,200 done properly with pump and seals; demand a dated receipt, not 'seller says it was done.' 2) Crank nose / crank keyway failure — the 'crank wobble' or short-nose crank issue on 1.6L cars (and some early 1.8s) where the pulley bolt loosens, chews the keyway and destroys the crank snout. Symptoms: wandering timing mark, clunk at idle, wobbling pulley. A trashed crank means engine-out, $2,500–$5,000. Ask whether the pulley bolt was re-torqued to spec (roughly 80–100 lb-ft plus) at the last belt job. 3) Rust — rear wheel arches, rocker panels, front frame rails behind the fenders, floor pans, and especially the rear frame rail near the differential mount and the battery tray corner. Northeast/Midwest cars are frequently structurally rotten under fresh paint. A California car should be clean; still check the rockers and the seam under the rear of the doors. 4) Soft top and rain leaks: original vinyl/cloth tops are 25+ years old, plastic rear windows craze and crack, and zippers fail. Patched tears (as in the example listing) mean a top is due: $400–$900 for a quality cloth top with glass window installed. Leaks track to clogged drain tubes behind the seats — water pools in the floor pans and rots them and the ECU area. 5) Cooling system: 30-year-old radiators (plastic end tanks), brittle hoses, failing thermostats and radiator caps. Overheating on a hot day is common and these engines are tolerant but not immortal. Budget $300–$600 for radiator, hoses, cap, thermostat. 6) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, front crank seal, cam seals, and rear main. The 'oil leak noted' in this listing is typical — valve cover $150, front seals with the timing belt job, rear main $600–$900 with trans out. 7) Suspension bushings and shocks: original bushings are shot at this age; sloppy rear subframe, worn ball joints, torn CV/axle boots, and dead OEM dampers. A full refresh with decent dampers and bushings runs $900–$2,000. 8) Differential and drivetrain: PPF bushings, worn differential mount, leaking diff and transmission seals, and the notorious 5th-gear/2nd-gear synchro wear on high-mile boxes. A crunchy 2nd gear cold is a warning; a rebuilt or used trans is $800–$1,800 installed. Also check the clutch slave cylinder (very common leak, $80 part) and master. 9) Electrics: pop-up headlight motors and linkage (slow or one-eye-up), failing window regulators/motors, worn ignition switch, aged main relay, cracked crank angle sensor O-ring leaking oil, and corroded grounds. Individually cheap, collectively annoying. 10) Interior degradation: sun-baked dashboards crack at the defroster vents, seat bolsters split (especially tan leather on Special Edition/M Edition cars), door card vinyl delaminates, and the plastic rear window scuffs. Dash cap or replacement $200–$600. 11) Brakes and fuel system: seized rear caliper slide pins and parking brake mechanisms, rusty hard lines on non-West-Coast cars, and original fuel pumps/filters that are well past service. 12) Modifications: many NAs have been autocrossed, lowered on cheap coilovers, or fitted with turbo kits. Aftermarket exhaust (as here) may not be CARB-legal for California registration; sway bars and roll bars are benign but raise the question of track use. Look for evidence of an untracked life. 13) Airbag/SRS and the 1990–93 short-nose crank plus 1.6L's smaller brakes are worth noting; 1994+ 1.8L cars gained more power, larger brakes and a stiffer chassis, but also the 1994–95 OBD-I/1996+ OBD-II split which affects California smog testing ease.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Timing belt/water pump/tensioner and front seals with a properly torqued crank pulley bolt if no dated receipt exists ($700–$1,200); full fluid service (engine oil, coolant flush, brake fluid, gear oil, diff oil, $300–$500); clutch slave cylinder and a look at the master ($150–$300); clean the soft-top drain tubes and reseal/replace the top if patched ($400–$900); radiator cap, thermostat and hoses if age-unknown ($200–$400); four fresh tires if the current set is over six years old regardless of tread ($500–$800); alignment after any suspension work ($120); fix the noted oil leak, usually valve cover gasket and front seals ($150–$400); new battery and a check of all grounds.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Shock/strut and bushing refresh including rear subframe, control arm and PPF bushings ($900–$2,000); rear main or transmission seal if a leak develops ($600–$900); clutch if it's original and slipping ($800–$1,200 with rear main done at the same time); pop-up headlight motor or linkage repair ($150–$400); window regulator/motor ($150–$300 per side); dash cap or dash replacement if cracked ($200–$600); seat re-bolstering or covers on leather cars ($400–$1,200); brake caliper rebuild/slide pin service and rotors/pads ($400–$700); possible fuel pump, CAS O-ring and ignition refresh (cap, rotor, wires, plugs, $200–$400); catalyst/exhaust restoration to CARB-legal configuration if California smog is a concern ($400–$1,200).
profiles.market_notes: NA prices are driven by rust-free bodies, dated timing belt receipts, originality, and color/trim rarity far more than mileage — clean drivers sit in the $8k–$15k band, sorted 1.8L R-package or low-mile survivors reach $18k–$30k+, and museum-grade 1990 launch cars or pristine BRG Special Editions can exceed that. The 1991 British Racing Green Special Edition (tan leather, Nardi wood, LSD, ~4,000 built) carries a modest premium over a base 1.6, but modifications, a patched top, a noted oil leak and only partial records pull it back toward driver money — which is exactly why the example car landed near $11k. Automatics, non-LSD cars, aftermarket body kits, turbo builds and anything with rocker/rail rust trade at a steep discount. In coastal California, smog-legality of the exhaust and a clean CA title in the seller's name are real value items.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 30-plus-year-old car needs a deferred-maintenance sweep regardless of mileage: all rubber (belts, hoses, bushings, seals), all fluids, tires by date code, the soft top and its drains, and the cooling system. Budget $2,000–$3,500 in the first year on a clean California example just to bring the consumables current, plus a contingency for a crank/timing surprise on a car with no belt receipt.

profiles.label: Mazda Rotary Pickup (REPU, 1974-1977)
profiles.framing: The REPU is the only rotary-powered pickup ever series-produced, sold only in North America, and roughly 15,000 were built with very few survivors that are not rusty, swapped, or both. For this buyer it is a weekend-and-errands novelty truck with real collector standing, not a load hauler: the 13B makes its case with a 7,000-rpm tach and a howl no small truck has any business making. What matters is a healthy (or honestly documented) rotary, a solid cab/bed/frame, and the survival of the REPU-only sheetmetal and trim that cannot be bought at any price. Engine swaps (13B-REW, 20B, LS) are common and can be well executed, but they change the car from 'documented original' to 'someone's build' and, in California, create a real registration problem.
profiles.weak_points: ['Apex seals and rotor housing wear are the defining risk. A tired 13B shows hard hot restarts, blue smoke on startup, low and uneven cranking compression, and a rough idle that smooths above 3,000 rpm. Insist on a rotary-specific compression test (Mazda-style tester reading all three faces per rotor at cranking speed, ideally at operating temperature): each face should be roughly 85-100 psi corrected with no more than about 10-15 psi spread between faces on the same rotor. A proper period 13B rebuild with new seals, re-nitrided or replacement housings, bearings and a rebuilt carb runs $6,000-10,000 today; a 20B or 13B-REW rebuild is $15,000-25,000 with parts that come from wrecked JDM cars.', 'Coolant seals and O-rings between the housings fail with any overheating event. Symptoms are unexplained coolant loss with no external leak, steam or sweet smell at the tailpipe, bubbles/pressure in the overflow, and a hot-start no-start. There is no head-gasket shortcut: it is a full teardown, so this failure is effectively the same cost as a rebuild. Ask for a cooling-system pressure test and a chemical block test for combustion gases in the coolant.', 'Cooling capacity was marginal when new and worse at 50 years old. Original copper/brass radiators are silted, the fan clutch is usually dead, and the thermostat and water pump housing are commonly corroded or cracked. Most healthy survivors have an aluminum radiator and electric fan; a stock-appearing truck with an unrecorded radiator history should be assumed to need a recore ($400-800) or aluminum replacement plus hoses and thermostat ($600-1,200 installed).', 'The thermal reactor exhaust system (a heat-shielded manifold that burned unburnt fuel to meet 1970s emissions) is a known fire and heat-soak hazard. Originals crack, glow red, cook the wiring and firewall insulation, and are effectively unobtainable ($2,000-4,000 if one surfaces). Most trucks have a header and a straight exhaust; that is a functional improvement but an originality loss, and any reactor-delete should be checked for heat shielding, brake line routing, and fuel line proximity.', "The Nikki four-barrel carburetor is the REPU-specific fuel-system weak point: dried accelerator pumps, worn secondary linkage, plugged idle circuits, a seized choke, and a hot-soak percolation problem that mimics flooding. Rebuild kits are scarce ($400-1,200 for a competent rebuild) and many trucks run Holley/Weber or EFI conversions. Ask what carb is fitted and whether idle/part-throttle air-fuel has actually been checked, not just 'it runs'.", "Oil metering pump (OMP) status is the single cheapest question with the biggest consequence. If the OMP has been blocked off or disconnected, the engine MUST be premixed (roughly 2-4 oz of two-stroke or 10W30 per gallon) at every fill, forever. Ask directly for the premix routine and receipts for oil; a blocked OMP plus a seller who says 'you don't need to premix' is an apex-seal timebomb. A functioning OMP should be verified for flow at the injection lines.", 'Rust is the usual reason a REPU is not worth saving. Check cab corners, the lower rear cab panel and rear window channel (the 1977 bumped-out window in particular traps water), floor pans under the rubber/carpet, the seat riser and cab mounts, the inner and outer bedsides behind the REPU-only flares, the front fender bottoms, the battery box on the right bedside (acid rot), and the frame rails at the rear spring hangers and above the axle. Cab corner and floor repair with correct fabrication is $3,000-8,000 in bodywork, and there are no reproduction REPU panels.', "REPU-only trim is unobtainium: the eggcrate grille, fender flares, round taillights, 'Rotary Pickup/Rotary Engine' badging and tailgate lettering, the rotary-specific instrument cluster with 7,000-rpm tach, the bumpers, and the 1977 rear-window glass. Missing or damaged pieces can cost thousands on the collector market or stall a project indefinitely. Photograph and inventory e
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service including a coolant flush with correct rotary-safe coolant; new thermostat, hoses, and cap; complete brake hydraulic refresh (flex lines, wheel cylinders or caliper seals, master, fluid); replace all rubber fuel line with SAE 30R9 and check the tank and sender; tires almost always need replacing on date code alone even with good tread; ignition tune (plugs, wires, points/condenser or coil check, timing set with a light on both leading and trailing); establish and document a premix routine if the OMP is blocked; belts, battery, and a full lighting/grounds sweep; leak-check the radiator and lower housing and plan an aluminum radiator/electric fan if the truck runs hot in traffic; seat belts and steering-play assessment before it is driven on Highway 1. Budget $3,000-6,000.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and rear main/front cover seals if the engine is out for anything; four-speed second-gear synchro or a documented five-speed conversion; leaf springs, shackle bushings, shocks, and U-joints; steering box and drag-link refresh; exhaust fabrication or heat shielding done properly; carburetor rebuild or a documented tune of whatever induction is fitted; localized rust repair at cab corners, bedsides, and battery box before it spreads; radiator recore; wiring harness repairs where heat has cooked the insulation; and a compression retest at the 12-month mark to trend seal health. Budget $4,000-9,000 on a good truck, far more if the engine has to come out.
profiles.market_notes: Condition and originality drive REPU money far more than mileage, which is unverifiable on a five-digit odometer and largely irrelevant on a rebuilt rotary. Rust-free Southwest/California survivors with complete REPU-only trim, original 13B, correct gauges, and a documented history are the top of the market; well-executed 20B/13B-REW builds with named builders and standalone tunes can match or exceed that number with a narrower buyer pool and no smog path in CA. Long-bed 1977 cars with the bumped-out rear window have their own following as the final-year variant. Discounts come fast for rust, missing grille/flares/taillights/badges, non-rotary swaps (LS), automatic conversions, and 'ran when parked' engines; expect roughly $20,000-30,000 for a driver, $35,000-55,000 for an excellent original or a strong documented build, and $60,000+ only for concours-grade originals.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume everything rubber and every fluid is due regardless of what the seller says: fuel hose, brake hydraulics, coolant, radiator, hoses, bushings, and tires on date code alone. A 50-year-old low-production Japanese truck also needs a wiring and grounds sweep and a fuel-tank inspection before it is trusted on a mountain road, and any rotary with unknown seal history should be priced with a rebuild reserve set aside from day one.

profiles.label: Porsche 911 (964) Carrera 2 / Carrera 4
profiles.framing: The 964 is the last usable-everyday air-cooled 911 with modern comforts (power steering, ABS, coil springs, real HVAC) and the raw M64 3.6 character that later cars smooth out. For a Carmel-based driver, this is a weekend Highway 1 and Laureles Grade car that can be driven hard without the anxiety of a six-figure 993 Turbo or a museum-grade 2.7 RS — but only if the engine's known sealing and top-end issues are documented as already addressed. The Carrera 4's extra driveline (front diff, transfer shaft, ABD/ABS hydraulics) adds capability and complexity; a well-sorted C4 is a superb all-weather coastal car, a neglected one is a money pit. Documented, unmodified, with a legible chain of invoices matters far more here than mileage or cosmetics.
profiles.weak_points: Engine case/cylinder oil leaks: the M64's biggest single issue is leaking head studs and, more famously, the dual-row-to-single-row era case and the notorious oil return tube and cylinder-to-case seepage. Most honest 964s weep from the through-bolt/head-stud area and the chain housing gaskets; a proper fix is engine-out, roughly $12,000–$25,000+ depending on whether cylinders/pistons and heads are touched. Look for an engine-out invoice naming head studs (ARP or Raceware), Carrillo/ARP rod bolts, and resealing of the chain housings and cam towers. Dual-mass flywheel: early cars (1989–1991) used a Freudenberg DMF that fails and clatters at idle; later LuK units are better. Failure symptoms are rattle at idle that disappears on clutch engagement; replacement is a transmission-out job, $2,500–$4,500 with clutch. Distributor vent belt (the internal belt linking the twin distributor rotors): if it snaps, the secondary rotor runs unsynchronized, torching the cap and potentially the engine. Later factory vented caps mitigate; there must be a receipt in the last 4–6 years / 30–40k miles or plan $600–$1,200 to inspect and renew. Valve guides and top-end wear: high-mileage M64s (over 100k) smoke on startup and burn oil; a leakdown/compression test is not optional. Head gaskets and studs pulling on high-heat, hard-driven cars are a five-figure repair. Oil cooler and lines: the front-fender-mounted oil cooler and long steel/rubber oil lines corrode and weep; a leaking cooler dumps oil quickly and costs $700–$1,800 plus lines. Air conditioning: original R12 systems converted poorly to R134a are the norm; condensers, evaporator, and hoses all age out and full restoration with a modern condenser/parallel-flow setup runs $2,000–$4,000. Carrera 4 specific: the front differential and transfer/center driveshaft leak and the ABD/PDAS hydraulic unit and its accumulator fail — a failed C4 hydraulic pump or pressure accumulator triggers ABS/brake warning lights and parts are scarce and expensive ($1,500–$4,000). C4 front CV/axle boots and the front driveshaft support are common leak points. Motor/transmission mounts sag (many owners fit 993-spec mounts, as this car has), causing shifter vibration. Suspension bushings, control-arm ball joints, and rear spring plate bushings are all 30 years old on original cars; a full refresh with Bilsteins runs $3,000–$6,000. Airbag/pedal box: the 964 pedal cluster bushings wear and the clutch pedal bracket cracks — a known and cheap-to-fix but commonly ignored item. Electrics: the alarm/central locking control unit, power window regulators, HVAC control head (blend flap servos and the vacuum-operated system) and instrument cluster board solder joints all fail; the odometer gears crack and the speedo needs a rebuild ($400–$800). Rust: 964s are galvanized and generally sound, but check the front trunk floor/battery tray, the sunroof drains and the A-pillar corners, the base of the windshield (leaks from resealed or replaced windshields cause rot under the dash), and the rear torsion tube area. Fuel system: rubber fuel hoses and the fuel-line rail under the tank harden; fire risk on cars without replacement records. Finally, at 150k+ miles the five-speed G64 transaxle's second-gear synchro wears — notchy 2nd on a cold car is normal, a crunch under load is not; a rebuild is $5,000–$8,000.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (Mobil 1 15W-50 or equivalent, ~11 quarts, filter, drain plug seals), valve adjustment if not documented within 15k miles, new fuel filter, inspect and likely replace the distributor vent belt and both caps/rotors if the receipt is older than five years, replace hardened fuel and vacuum hoses, four-wheel alignment after any suspension work, check and correct tire age (anything over six years replaced regardless of tread), A/C evacuate/recharge and leak test, and a full diagnostic scan of the DME and — on a C4 — the ABS/ABD hydraulic system. Expect to chase at least one small oil leak (chain housing, oil return tubes, or a cooler line) and to service or rebuild the pedal box bushings.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and dual-mass flywheel if not recently replaced, motor and transmission mounts if still original, front and rear shock/strut refresh and rubber bushings if undocumented, oil cooler and hard lines if any seepage, A/C condenser and hoses for reliable coastal-summer function, power window regulators and central locking control unit, HVAC blend/flap servos, brake flex lines and full fluid flush (and ABS accumulator on the C4 if pressure warning appears), and on higher-mileage cars a transaxle reseal and possible 2nd-gear synchro attention. Budget for a set of correct-size Michelin or Pirelli N-rated tires and a proper corner-balance/alignment.
profiles.market_notes: Coupes with a manual outsell Tiptronics by a wide margin and Tiptronic C2s trade at a steep discount; Carrera 4 coupes historically sat below C2s but factory widebody (Turbo-look, option M491) cars are genuinely rare and command a large premium, as do RS Americas, Turbos, and Speedsters. Documented engine-out top-end work with head studs is worth real money and its absence should be priced in at $15,000–$25,000 regardless of how the car presents. Original paint and matching numbers matter, but a well-executed, fully invoiced refurbishment with photos from a known shop is acceptable to a driver-buyer; unverifiable 'restored' claims, respray over filler, and mileage discrepancies (or a Carfax that misidentifies the model, as in the example listing) are where money is lost. High-mileage cars are acceptable at the right price if the service chain is continuous; six-figure asks on a 170k-mile C4 rest entirely on the quality and verifiability of the rebuild paperwork.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 30-plus-year-old 964 needs everything rubber renewed: fuel and vacuum hoses, brake flex lines, engine and transmission mounts, suspension bushings, window and door seals, and the A/C system. Even a freshly refurbished example will need a shakedown cycle of fluid services, a valve adjustment, alignment, and chasing small leaks over the first few thousand miles, plus tires if the date codes are past six years.

profiles.label: Porsche 944 Turbo / Turbo S (951, 1986–1991)
profiles.framing: The 951 is the sharpest-driving front-engine Porsche of the era: 2.5L turbo four, rear transaxle, near-50/50 balance, and in Turbo S trim the M030 suspension, 40% limited-slip, and 928 S4 brakes that make it genuinely quick on a real road. For a Carmel-based driver this is a weekend-and-occasional-commute car that rewards mechanical sympathy and punishes deferred maintenance more than almost anything else from the 1980s. What matters is not mileage on the odometer but the last five years of receipts: belts, rollers, water pump, cooling system, torque tube, and a clean compression/leak-down. Coastal humidity and salt-air storage mean the battery box, sunroof drains, and hatch surround deserve as much attention as the engine.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt and balance-shaft belt with their rollers and tensioner: the M44/52 is an interference engine and a snapped or jumped belt bends valves and can crack the head — budget $6,000–12,000 for the repair versus $900–1,800 for the preventive service. Service interval is realistically 30,000 miles or 4 years regardless of miles; demand a dated, mileage-stamped invoice, ideally with a belt-tension-gauge reading noted. Low-mileage cars are the highest risk here because owners defer on miles, not years. 2) Water pump and thermostat housing: pumps seize or leak from the weep hole and take the timing belt with them — always replaced with belts; plastic/alloy housings and the coolant crossover corrode. 3) Cylinder head cracking between the valve seats and head-gasket failure on any car that has been overheated or run lean/overboosted — symptoms are coolant loss with no external leak, pressurized expansion tank, sweet exhaust smell. A used head plus machine work and gasket set runs $3,500–6,000. 4) Oil cooler O-rings/seals at the block leak oil into coolant or coolant into oil — look for mayonnaise on the filler cap and at the cooler seams; a straightforward $400–800 job if caught early. 5) Turbocharger: K26/6 (Turbo) or K26/8 (Turbo S) shaft play, coked oil feed line, and failing oil return gasket cause blue smoke on overrun and boost loss. Rebuilt cartridges/units run $1,500–3,000 installed; the oil feed line should be replaced any time the turbo is. 6) Boost-control system: the wastegate diaphragm, KLR cycling valve, and a web of aging rubber vacuum and boost hoses crack and cause soft boost, overboost cutout, or surge. A full silicone/rubber hose refresh and wastegate rebuild is $400–1,200. 7) Torque tube bearings and center support: a resonant droning/whirring at 2,000–3,500 rpm that changes with clutch engagement; rebuild or replacement is $1,500–3,500 because the transaxle and tube must come out. 8) Clutch: the rubber-centered disc degrades with age and the pressure plate/pilot bearing go with it; do the torque tube, rear main seal, and clutch together — $2,500–4,500 as a package. 9) Front suspension: the one-piece control arms with integral ball joints and the aging bushings produce vague steering and clunks; arms are $300–700 each plus alignment. Turbo S Koni adjustables often seize or leak and are expensive to replace or rebuild ($1,200–2,500 for a set). Rear torsion bar tube bushings and seized torsion adjusters make ride-height correction a job. 10) Brakes: Turbo S (and 1989 Turbo) use 928 S4 four-piston calipers and larger rotors — parts are pricier and some rotors are becoming scarce; seized pistons and crusty ABS lines are common on stored cars. Full four-corner refresh with rotors and rebuilt calipers is $2,000–3,500. The Bosch ABS system's sensors and the hydraulic unit can be costly and hard to source. 11) Electrical gremlins: the DME/fuel pump relay is a classic no-start, ground strap corrosion causes random faults, and the VDO instrument cluster's odometer gears strip — which is exactly why so many 944s carry 'Not Actual Mileage' or mileage-inconsistency entries. A branded NAM title is permanent and materially affects value. 12) Interior consumables: cracked dash pads ($800–2,000 to replace/recover), sagging headliner and sunroof cassette, failing window regulators and motors, disintegrating door-card and rear-hatch trim, and vacuum-operated HVAC controls that stop working when the pod diaphragms fail. 13) Air conditioning: original R12 systems either converted or dead; evaporator replacement means dash-out labor at $1,500–2,500. 14) Rust and water: bodies are galvanized so rot is not endemic, but check the battery box and the floor/frame rail under it (acid), sunroof drain exits, the rear hatch surround and hinge area, the fuel tank/torsion tube area, jack points, and the inner fenders behind the front wheels. Also inspect for aged fuel hoses under the intake and at the fuel rail — 1980s rubber plus turbo h
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service if not documented within 12 months (engine oil, transaxle, brake fluid, coolant); DME and fuel pump relay replacement plus a spare; replacement of any rubber fuel line under the intake and at the rail; rubber/vacuum and boost hose refresh with new clamps; tires if older than 6 years regardless of tread (very common on low-use 951s); battery, ground straps, and a battery-box cleanup; front-end alignment; and if belt documentation is thin or older than 4 years, an immediate timing/balance belt, roller, tensioner, water pump and thermostat service. Expect $2,500–5,000 in the first 30 days on a typical documented car and more if belts are unknown.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch, rear main seal, and torque tube bearings as a combined job if any driveline drone or clutch shudder is present; oil cooler seals and valve-cover/cam-tower gasket leaks; wastegate diaphragm and boost-control refresh; brake caliper rebuild plus rotors and stainless lines; Koni damper rebuild or replacement and rear torsion-bar bushings; motor and transaxle mounts; A/C recharge or evaporator/condenser work; window regulator and sunroof mechanism service; and cosmetic catch-up on dash, seat bolsters, and rear hatch struts. A realistic 12-month figure is $4,000–9,000 depending on what the PPI finds.
profiles.market_notes: The 1988 Turbo S (about 1,000 US cars, including the Silver Rose edition) and the 1989 Turbo that inherited S mechanicals sit well above standard 1986–1988 Turbos, and a Porsche Certificate of Authenticity confirming S equipment is effectively required to claim the premium. Documented belt/water-pump service, original paint, correct 16" Club Sport wheels, a working A/C, and unmolested boost/ECU are the value drivers; chipped/overboosted cars, cut dashes, and aftermarket turbo or intercooler swaps push buyers away. Mileage bands matter but only when the odometer is credible — a 'Not Actual Mileage' or mileage-inconsistency brand should discount a car meaningfully (commonly 15–30%) versus an equivalent clean-title example, because it is permanent and follows the car. Manual-only market; color and interior condition (especially an uncracked dash and unfaded leatherette) swing the last 10%.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 35-plus-year-old car needs a rubber and fluid reset regardless of mileage: every vacuum, boost, coolant, and fuel hose, belts and pump on age not miles, tires, brake fluid and flexlines, and motor mounts. Low-mileage examples are often worse in this respect than driven ones — seals dry out, fuel systems varnish, and Konis seize from sitting. Budget $3,000–6,000 of age-related catch-up in year one even on a well-presented car.

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster (981, incl. S / GTS / Spyder)
profiles.framing: The 981 is the sweet spot of modern Boxsters: the last naturally aspirated flat-six mid-engine Porsche roadster, with electric steering that is still genuinely good, a stiff aluminum-intensive chassis, and no IMS bearing to worry about. For a Carmel-based driver this is a near-ideal Highway 1 / Laureles Grade weekend car that can also be driven daily in the region's mild climate, with the caveat that it is a two-seat convertible with two small trunks. What matters here is a documented, unmodified-or-reversible example with a full Porsche/independent service file, a healthy convertible top mechanism, and evidence the engine has never been abused or run low on oil; the 9A1 flat-six is a strong motor but a bad one is a five-figure problem.
profiles.weak_points: ['Bore scoring / cylinder scuffing on the 9A1 DFI flat-six is uncommon but not extinct, and it is the single catastrophic risk. Symptoms are ticking or knocking at cold start that fades as it warms, oil consumption worse than roughly 1 qt / 1,200 miles, and a faint sooty smell. It shows up most often on hard-driven or short-tripped cars past 60-80k miles. A borescope of all six cylinders plus a DME over-rev report is the only real protection; an engine replacement or rebuild is $18,000-$28,000+.', 'Cracked cylinder heads / coolant loss on early 9A1 engines (mostly 2013-2014) present as slow, unexplained coolant level drop with no visible external leak, sometimes with a sweet smell after a hard drive. Check the expansion tank level history in service records and pressure-test the cooling system. Head or engine work is $8,000-$20,000.', 'Water pump with a composite impeller typically fails between 60k and 100k miles or roughly 8-10 years; symptoms are weeping from the pump area, coolant smell, or temperature creep in traffic. Budget $1,100-$1,800 done properly with a thermostat and coolant service. On a 78k-mile 2014 with no pump record, assume it is due.', 'Coolant expansion tank and its cap crack with age, and the plastic coolant hard lines / hose connectors get brittle. Look for dried pink-orange crust in the engine bay and at the rear of the block. $400-$900.', 'Air-oil separator (AOS) diaphragm failure causes a big puff of blue smoke at startup or after a highway pull, rough idle, and oil consumption. Typical at 70k-100k miles; $700-$1,200 installed. Frequently misdiagnosed as bore scoring, so a proper crankcase vacuum test is worth insisting on.', 'Rear main seal and, less often, the case-half seam weep oil onto the transaxle bellhousing. A light film is common; drips that require topping off mean pulling the transaxle, which is a $2,000-$3,500 job unless combined with a clutch.', 'Manual cars: dual-mass flywheel and clutch. Judder from a stop, high engagement point, or a rattle at idle that disappears with the clutch depressed means DMF. Replacement with flywheel and rear main seal while you are in there runs $3,000-$4,500. Most 981 manuals go 80k-120k miles, so a 78k car is inside the window.', 'PDK cars: the 60k-mile / 6-year mechatronic fluid and filter service is $700-$1,100 and is skipped constantly. A missing PDK service record on a 70k+ car is a real negotiating point; mechatronic unit failure is $5,000-$9,000.', 'Convertible top: the drive cables, hydraulic pump lines, tensioning bow bushings, microswitches, and the rear window seam are all wear items. Symptoms are a top that stalls mid-cycle, a warning message, or a hydraulic fluid smell/stain in the rear trunk area. Cable or hydraulic repairs run $1,200-$2,500; a full top replacement is $2,800-$4,500. Always cycle the top three or four times, fully, before buying.', "Clogged convertible-top and cowl drains flood the footwells and the area under the seats where control modules live. Look for damp carpet padding, musty smell, corroded seat rail hardware, or a car with a recent 'electrical gremlin' history. Water-damaged modules are $800-$2,500 each.", 'PASM dampers (standard on S/GTS, optional on base) start weeping and losing damping between 70k and 100k miles; you get a chassis warning or clunking over expansion joints. OEM dampers are $700-$1,300 per corner installed. Aftermarket coilovers on a listing usually mean the originals were tired.', 'A/C condensers sit in the front corners behind the radiators and collect leaves, sand, and salt; in a coastal environment they corrode and leak refrigerant, and the same debris rots the radiators. Expect $900-$1,800 to replace condensers and clean the ducting. Ask for photos of the front corner ducts with the liners out.', 'Bi-xenon / PDLS headlight units and ballasts fail with age and are expensive: $1,200-$2,200 per side for OEM. A car with recently replaced headlights (as in this example) has already eaten that cost, w
profiles.immediate_repairs: ['Full fluid catch-up: engine oil with genuine filter, brake fluid flush (2-year interval, almost always overdue), coolant condition check and pressure test', 'Tires: replace non-N-spec or over-5-year-old staggered set with N-rated rubber, plus alignment ($1,600-$2,200)', 'Cooling system: water pump and thermostat if there is no record within 60k miles ($1,100-$1,800)', 'Convertible top service: lubricate mechanism, clear cowl and top drains, check hydraulic lines and rear window seam ($300-$700, more if cables are stretched)', 'Battery test/replace with proper coding if the car sat or is on its original AGM ($400-$600)', 'Exhaust: verify smog compliance for California registration; source and reinstall factory exhaust if cats were deleted ($1,200-$2,500)', 'PIWIS fault-code clear and re-s
profiles.repairs_12mo: ['Clutch and dual-mass flywheel on a manual approaching 90-100k miles ($3,000-$4,500) or PDK mechatronic service if not documented ($700-$1,100)', 'Air-oil separator if oil consumption or startup smoke develops ($700-$1,200)', 'PASM damper replacement if weeping or if ride quality is degraded ($2,800-$4,500 for four)', 'A/C condenser replacement and front duct cleanout, typical for coastal cars ($900-$1,800)', 'Spark plugs and coils at the 4-year/40k interval ($600-$1,000)', 'Engine and transmission mounts if idle shudder is present ($600-$1,200)', 'Soft-top rear window or full top replacement if the seam is delaminating ($2,800-$4,500)', 'Suspension refresh items: control arm bushings, sway bar links, and a corner-balance alignment ($800-$1,600)']
profiles.market_notes: Transmission and engine drive the money: a 6-speed manual commands a clear premium over PDK in the enthusiast market, and Boxster S / GTS 3.4 cars trade several thousand above a 2.7 base regardless of options. Spec matters at the margins - Sport Chrono with PSE, adaptive sport seats, PASM, a non-black interior, and a genuinely interesting exterior color lift a car; base cloth-spec silver/white/black cars with 19s and no options sit. Records are worth real money on this generation: a folder showing water pump, PDK or clutch service, brake fluid history, and no accidents will beat a lower-mileage undocumented car with a damage entry. Aftermarket exhaust, non-N-spec tires, and a Carfax damage report each shave value, and mileage bands break roughly at 40k, 70k, and 100k.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-12 year old, 70-80k mile 981 needs a deferred-maintenance sweep even when it looks perfect: brake fluid, coolant, plugs and coils, AGM battery with coding, water pump if undocumented, N-spec tires, and a convertible top lubrication and drain cleanout. Coastal Monterey cars additionally want the front duct liners pulled to clean debris off the radiators and condensers before corrosion sets in. Plan $3,000-$5,000 of catch-up in the first year on top of the purchase price, separate from the clutch/DMF or PDK service that lurks in the next 20k miles.

Lift carpet/check under seats for damp padding, corrosion, musty smell; clear top and cowl drains

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster / Boxster S (987.1 & 987.2)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 987 is a mid-engine, open-top back-road car for Highway 1, Carmel Valley Road and the occasional track day — not a garage investment. It is one of the last analog, hydraulically-assisted Porsches available at commuter-car money, and a well-documented manual example is a genuinely usable daily driver with a frunk plus trunk. The entire buying decision hinges on engine provenance: 987.1 cars (2005–2008, M96/M97) carry IMS bearing and bore-scoring risk that can turn a $16k car into a $30k car overnight, while 987.2 cars (2009–2012, 9A1 DFI) eliminate both. Coastal humidity and salt air matter less than rust-belt exposure, but clogged convertible-top and cowl drains cause expensive electrical damage in any climate.
profiles.weak_points: 1) IMS bearing (2005–2008 M96/M97 only): 2005 and very early 2006 engines use the smaller single-row bearing with the highest failure rate; engines built from roughly mid-2006 through 2008 use a larger non-serviceable bearing with a lower failure rate but which cannot be retrofitted without splitting the engine. A proactive IMS retrofit (LN Engineering ceramic hybrid or IMS Solution) done with clutch and RMS runs $3,000–$4,500 and should be documented by invoice with the engine number. Absence of a retrofit is not a dealbreaker on a 2006+ car but is a $3.5k line item. 2) Bore scoring: most common on the 3.4 M97 (2007–2008 S) but present on 2.7s too; symptoms are cold-start rattle/ticking that fades, elevated oil consumption (worse than ~1 qt/1,000 mi), and a smoky start after sitting. Only a borescope through the spark plug holes proves cylinder condition — this is the single most valuable pre-purchase test. A scored engine means a $12,000–$20,000 rebuild or used-engine swap. 3) Rear main seal (RMS) weeping: nearly universal at some level; a light film is normal, active dripping onto the bellhousing means $1,500–$2,000 alone or fold it into a clutch/IMS job. 4) Air/oil separator (AOS) diaphragm failure at 60k–100k miles: huge white smoke cloud at startup, rough idle, oil pulled into intake; $600–$1,200 installed. 5) Water pump with plastic impeller: typical life 60k–80k miles; impeller blades shed and clog the system, $700–$1,100. Do it with the thermostat and coolant. 6) Coolant expansion tank cracks and cap failure at 10–15 years, $700–$1,200; look for dried pink/orange crust in the engine bay and under the rear. 7) Front radiators and A/C condensers: leaves and debris pack the lower ducts, holding moisture against aluminum until the condensers corrode through — extremely common on 12–20 year old cars. Full front radiator/condenser refresh with grilles is $1,500–$2,800. 8) Convertible top: transmission cables fray and the plastic drive blocks/rollers break, the hydraulic pump and rams leak onto the trunk carpet, the microswitches and the rear window seam fail. Top mechanism work is $1,000–$2,500; a new top with window is $2,000–$3,500. 9) Blocked top and cowl drains: water backs up into the footwells and into the seat/convertible-top control modules and under-seat wiring — causes dash warnings, dead tops, and mildew. Pull the carpet edges and check for staining. 10) Suspension wear at 70k+ miles: front lower control arms (including the rear 'coffin' arm bushings), front and rear top mounts, and tie rods; a full corner refresh is $1,500–$3,000. Sagging ride height and clunks over expansion joints are the tell. 11) Clutch and dual-mass flywheel on 100k-mile manuals: $2,500–$3,500 done properly with RMS and IMS access. Judder from a stop is the DMF. 12) Variocam actuators/solenoids and chain-pad wear on M96/M97: a rattle for 1–3 seconds on cold start plus cam deviation values out of spec on a Durametric scan; actuator/solenoid work $1,200–$2,500. 13) Electrical annoyances: ignition switch failure, door lock/latch microswitches (door won't unlock, top won't operate), airbag light from the passenger seat occupancy mat ($600–$1,000 for the mat), and PCM2 unit/CD-changer failures. 14) Tiptronic (5-speed auto in 987.1) and PDK (987.2): the Tiptronic is durable but dulls the car badly and hurts resale; PDK mechatronic and clutch-pack service is expensive out of warranty ($3,000+). 987.2 DFI engines are far more robust but are known for occasional high-pressure fuel pump and injector issues and for coolant-pipe/thermostat housing seepage.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluids service (Mobil 1 0W-40 with a genuine filter, brake fluid, coolant top-up), four correct-size tires if mismatched or over 6 years old, front radiator/condenser duct cleaning and grille installation, convertible-top and cowl drain clearing, serpentine belt and tensioner if undocumented, battery if unknown age, and an alignment. Budget $1,200–$2,500. If the borescope or oil filter cut shows anything marginal, stop and renegotiate rather than repairing.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if there is no receipt in the last 60k miles, AOS if there is any startup smoke or idle hunt, coolant expansion tank on any 15+ year old car, front control arms and top mounts, a clutch/DMF plus IMS retrofit combined job on a 987.1 approaching 100k miles, convertible top transmission cables or hydraulic ram seals, and typically one electrical gremlin (ignition switch, door latch microswitch, or seat occupancy mat). Realistic 12-month spend on an unsorted 2006: $3,000–$6,000.
profiles.market_notes: Manual transmission is worth a clear premium over Tiptronic and is close to mandatory for resale; S models (3.2 then 3.4) carry roughly a 15–25% premium over base 2.7s, and 987.2 DFI cars command a further step up because they have no IMS and no meaningful bore-scoring reputation. Documented IMS retrofit, recent clutch, and a clean borescope report can add $2,000–$4,000 of buyer confidence on a 987.1. Color and options move money more than mileage below 100k: Guards Red, Cobalt/Aqua Blue, Speed Yellow and GT Silver with sport seats, PASM, Sport Chrono, litronics and a hardtop sell fastest, while black-on-black base cars with automatics are the soft end. Boxster Spyder and RS 60 Spyder trade in their own, much higher tier.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 15–20 year old 987.1 arrives needing rubber and plastic more than metal: coolant expansion tank, water pump, AOS, serpentine belt and tensioner, engine and top-mechanism seals, convertible-top cables and drain hoses, and front suspension bushings — plus tires and brake fluid regardless of tread and pedal feel. Assume $2,500–$4,000 of deferred catch-up in the first year even on a nicely kept car, and treat any clutch job as the right moment to bundle IMS, RMS, and flywheel work.
