profiles.label: Porsche Cayenne S (958.1, 2011–2014)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 958.1 Cayenne S is the do-everything Carmel car: a 400hp naturally aspirated 4.8 V8 with a genuinely good 8-speed Tiptronic, air suspension, all-wheel drive, and enough room for dogs, luggage, and a Highway 1 weekend. It is not an investment — depreciation has already done its work, and these trade around $15k–$25k regardless of how nice they are — so the whole game is buying the cheapest possible future maintenance rather than the cheapest possible car. A documented, one- or two-owner, non-air-suspension-failing example with cooling, suspension, and driveline receipts is worth a $5,000 premium over a bargain car, because that is roughly the delta in first-year repairs. Rust is a non-issue in coastal California; deferred German maintenance is the entire risk.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Coolant pipe / thermostat housing and water pump: the 4.8 V8's plastic coolant distribution components and the water pump are wear items typically due by 80–100k miles. Symptoms are low coolant warnings, sweet smell after shutdown, and crusty orange residue at the front/valley of the engine. Water pump plus thermostat runs $1,200–$2,200; a coolant pipe or crossover job that requires intake removal can hit $3,000+. Look for a receipt naming 'water pump' and 'thermostat' within the last 40k miles.

2) Air suspension (standard on most S cars, as on this example): rubber air struts crack with age/ozone and the compressor then runs itself to death trying to keep up. Symptoms are the car sitting low or nose-down overnight, 'Level Control Fault / Chassis Malfunction' messages, or the compressor audibly running at every start. OE Porsche struts are $1,200–$1,800 each installed; a compressor and valve block is $700–$1,200; a full four-corner refresh can exceed $6,000. On a 2011–2014 car that has never had struts replaced, assume this is a when-not-if item. Ask for the overnight ride-height video and any struts/compressor invoices.

3) Transfer case (the 958's biggest sleeper cost): the electronically controlled multi-plate clutch transfer case wears its clutch pack and servo motor, typically 70–120k miles. Symptoms are binding or shudder in tight low-speed turns, a 'PSM/4WD Failure' or 'Transfer Case Fault' message, driveline clunk, or a stored fault for the servo. Porsche does not rebuild it — a new unit is $4,000–$6,500 installed, and rebuild specialists run $2,500–$3,500. Mismatched or badly worn tires accelerate failure; check that all four tires are the same brand, model, and within ~2/32" of each other.

4) Driveshaft center support bearing and flex discs: a hum or vibration at 45–70 mph or a shudder from a stop. The driveshaft is often sold as a complete assembly; $1,200–$2,200 installed.

5) Rear differential and rear cover/bushing leaks, plus the Cayenne's habit of weeping from the transfer case output seal onto the rear driveshaft. Wipe the underside and look for fresh wet fluid versus old dry film.

6) 4.8 V8 oil consumption and valve cover / cam cover gasket seepage: some consumption is normal (up to ~1qt/1,000 mi Porsche considers acceptable), but heavy consumption with blue puff on cold start can indicate bore scoring on high-mile or hard-used examples. Bore scoring is rare on the 958 N/A 4.8 compared with the 955/957 era but not unheard of; a borescope of cylinders during PPI is cheap insurance and a scored engine is a $12,000+ walk-away.

7) Direct injection carbon buildup on intake valves: 80k+ cars often show rough cold idle, misfire codes at light load, and reduced mid-range. Walnut blasting is $900–$1,600 and is not in most service histories — treat as likely-due if there's no record.

8) Starter, alternator, and the buried-under-the-intake serviceability tax: nearly everything on the V8 top end requires intake removal, so labor multiplies. A starter that would be $400 on a Toyota is $1,200–$1,800 here.

9) PCM/electronics: the 2011–2014 PCM 3.1 head units suffer dead nav discs/SD readers, failed Bose amp channels, and delaminating touchscreens. Also check the panoramic/regular sunroof drains and the rear hatch strut/power liftgate motor. Aftermarket head unit swaps are common and often hide a failed OE unit.

10) Front suspension bushings and control arms: thrust arm and lower control arm bushings go 70–110k miles, producing clunks over expansion joints and wandering. Full front arms both sides $1,400–$2,400.

11) Brakes: 958 rotors are large and tend to crack around the vents and lip on stop-start use; a full four-corner rotor and pad job with sensors is $1,800–$3,000 at OE, less with quality aftermarket. Check rotor thickness and edge lip, not just pad life.

12) 21" wheels (as on the example car) with 295/35 tires: harsh ride, bent-rim risk on bad pavement, and a $1,600–$2,400 tire bill every 25–30k miles. Cu
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up (engine oil, brake fluid, coolant condition check, transfer case and differential fluids, Tiptronic fluid and filter if no record); battery test and replacement with registration; four matched tires if the set is mismatched or aged past 6 years; fresh alignment; sunroof drain flush; likely front thrust-arm bushings or a rattling sway bar link; wiper blades, cabin filter, engine air filters. Budget $2,000–$4,000 in the first 30 days on a typical 80k-mile example, more if the tire set must be replaced.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if not documented in the last 40k miles; one or two air struts and quite possibly the compressor and relay; walnut blasting for intake carbon; brake rotors and pads at all four corners; driveshaft center support bearing if a 50–70 mph hum is present; front lower control arms; possible transfer case service or replacement if any low-speed binding was noted at PPI. Realistic 12-month range for a well-bought car is $3,500–$7,000; a neglected one can double that.
profiles.market_notes: The 958.1 Cayenne S sits in a narrow $14k–$26k band where condition and records matter far more than options — clean-Carfax, two-owner, California cars with a service binder and no air-suspension faults live at the top, and any 'sold as-is with lights on' car lands at the bottom regardless of spec. The S (4.8 V8) is the sweet spot: better sound and simpler than the Turbo, dramatically more desirable than the V6 base, and without the Hybrid's battery risk; the rare 958.1 Cayenne S with a manual is a curiosity, not a value driver here. Color and interior move money modestly — white/black/grey over black or cognac sells easiest, and an unusual combination like Cream and Umber with birch trim adds interest but narrows the buyer pool. 21" wheels look good and cost money; smaller 18"/19" wheels are arguably a value-add for a real-world driver, and documented recent air struts, water pump, or transfer case work is worth more than any option code.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 10–14 year old, 80k-mile 958.1 is due for essentially everything the factory called 'lifetime': transmission fluid and filter, transfer case and differential fluids, coolant, brake fluid, and usually a battery. Rubber-based systems — air struts, control arm bushings, coolant hoses, engine mounts — age out on calendar rather than mileage, so even a low-mile California car should be budgeted as if it had 90k on it.

profiles.label: Porsche Cayenne Turbo (955, 4.5L twin-turbo V8)
profiles.framing: This is a 450-hp, 5,200-lb German luxury SUV that now trades for beater-Camry money precisely because the deferred maintenance bill can exceed the purchase price. For a Carmel-based buyer it makes sense only as a cheap, capable, weather-proof second vehicle — Highway 1 in the rain, Sierra ski trips, Big Sur fire roads — bought with eyes open and a funded repair reserve, never as an economy car. What matters is not the odometer but whether the coolant pipes, driveshaft, air suspension and propshaft/transfer case work has already been done with paper to prove it; a 47k-mile untouched example is arguably riskier than a 110k-mile one with a documented pipe job. Low mileage on a 20-year-old 955 mostly means aged rubber, plastic and seals, not a young car.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Plastic coolant crossover pipes under the intake manifold (the defining 955 Turbo failure). The factory used glued plastic Y-pipes and coolant tubes in the valley; they embrittle with heat cycling and let go — sometimes catastrophically at speed, which can cook the alloy block. Symptoms are coolant smell, weeping from the two telltale drain holes at the bellhousing, and low-coolant warnings. The fix is aluminum replacement pipes (Pelican/Sharkwerks/Dansk-style kits), $2,500–$4,500 with intake and turbo plumbing off; on a Turbo it is more labor than on an NA. Look for an invoice with line items for 'coolant pipes,' 'valley pipes,' or 'aluminum coolant tube upgrade,' plus photos taken with the intake off. No borescope, no invoice = assume it's due. 2) Driveshaft (propshaft) center support bearing and flex joints, typically 60k–100k miles or by age. Vibration at 40–60 mph, clunk on throttle transitions. Porsche sells only the complete shaft; $1,500–$2,500 installed, or rebuilt center bearing by a specialist for $600–$1,000. 3) Transfer case — the 955's electronically shifted case with dual-range and variable center diff. The servo motor and internal chain/clutch wear; symptoms are 'Transfer Case Fault' or 'Low Range Fault' in the dash, ABS/PSM lights, driveline binding, or a case that won't leave low. Servo motor rebuild $400–$900; complete used/reman case $2,000–$4,500 installed. Fluid is 'lifetime' and almost never changed — ask for it. 4) Air suspension: rear air springs and front struts crack and leak (car sits down overnight or on one corner), compressor then runs itself to death, and the valve block/level sensors fail. Individual bag $500–$900 per corner installed; compressor $500–$1,200; a full corner-by-corner rehab easily $3,000+. PASM shocks are separate and expensive. 5) Turbo/exhaust side: cracked exhaust manifolds and broken manifold-to-turbo studs on 4.5 twin-turbos, plus turbo oil-return leaks and wastegate/vacuum actuator faults. Blue smoke on startup, boost under-target codes, ticking cold. Manifold/stud work $1,500–$3,000; a turbo cartridge or pair $3,000–$6,000+. 6) Ignition and secondary air: eight coils and plugs are a wear item every ~60k or 10 years ($600–$1,000); secondary air injection pump and combi-valves stick and set P0410-family codes that will fail smog in California ($700–$1,800). 7) Cardan/front differential and front axle output seals leak; the front diff mounting bushings on the sump can allow diff movement. 8) Cooling accessories: thermostat housing, water pump (composite impeller), radiator end tanks and the plastic coolant reservoir all age out at 15–20 years; budget $1,200–$2,500 as a package if none of it is documented. 9) Electrical gremlins from the twin batteries/alternator and corroded grounds — the 955 is very voltage-sensitive and a weak battery produces a Christmas tree of faults (PSM, transfer case, air suspension) that clear with a good battery. A July 2023 battery on a car that sits is already suspect. 10) Interior: sticky soft-touch coatings on switchgear and the center console, sagging headliner, failed PCM/CD units, non-functioning HVAC blend-motor clicking, and cracked dash tops. Aftermarket head units (like a Dynavin) often mean a factory PCM failed or the CAN-integrated OEM unit was ripped out — check that the radio removal didn't break OBC/telephone functions. 11) Brakes: 350mm+ rotors and huge pads, $1,200–$2,000 for four corners with rotors; low-mileage cars almost always have rust-pitted or warped rotors from sitting. 12) Tires and alignment: a 20-year-old low-mile car will have date-coded-out rubber regardless of tread; a lifted, small-wheel, all-terrain conversion like this listing needs a fresh alignment and can throw PSM/ride-height calibration off. 13) Fuel economy and consumables are genuinely brutal — 13–15 mpg real world on premium, and the Turbo's parts pricing is 911 money on a 5,200-lb truck. 14) On lifted/off-road-converted cars, verify the air suspension
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up (engine oil, coolant if unknown, transfer case, front and rear diff, brake fluid, power steering, ZF Tiptronic service if no record) $900–$1,800. New battery and a proper charging-system/parasitic-draw check $300–$500. Four new date-coded tires and an alignment $1,100–$1,600. Full diagnostic scan on PIWIS/Durametric across all modules with printout, plus a borescope look at the valley coolant pipes if no invoice exists. Brake rotors and pads front and rear on a sat-a-lot car $1,200–$2,000. Air suspension leak-down test and likely at least one air spring $600–$1,000. Spark plugs and any weeping coils if older than 10 years $600–$1,000. On a modified example, either revert the lift/bumper to stock or budget the labor to verify fitment, ride-height calibration and sensor f
profiles.repairs_12mo: Coolant pipe conversion to aluminum if not already documented $2,500–$4,500. Driveshaft center bearing or complete shaft $800–$2,500. Thermostat, water pump, reservoir and hoses as an age-based package $1,200–$2,500. Secondary air pump/valves to pass California smog $700–$1,800. Transfer case servo or fluid-and-inspect, with reman case as the tail risk $500–$4,500. Air suspension compressor and remaining corners $1,000–$3,000. Exhaust manifold studs/gaskets and turbo oil-line seals $1,000–$3,000. Suspension bushings, control arms and sway bar links from age $1,000–$2,000. Interior fixes: headliner, sticky-plastic switchgear, HVAC blend motors $500–$1,500.
profiles.market_notes: 955 Turbos are near the bottom of their depreciation curve — running, sorted examples trade roughly $8k–$16k, with unsorted or high-mileage cars at $4k–$8k and exceptional low-mile documented cars occasionally to $20k+; Turbo S and the rare late-955 cars carry a modest premium. Price is driven almost entirely by documentation of the big-ticket items (coolant pipes, driveshaft, transfer case, air suspension) rather than by mileage; a $6k car with none of that work is a $12k car in disguise. Manual transmission was never offered on the Turbo, so Tiptronic is correct and not a demerit. Overland/lift conversions narrow the buyer pool and add unknowns — stock, unmodified, well-optioned (PCM, comfort seats, factory air suspension in good order) cars in conservative colors over black or stone gray sell best; California cars avoid the corroded fastener and rusty subframe misery of salt states and are worth seeking out.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any 955 Turbo as a 20-year-old car first and a low-mileage car second: rubber, plastic, coolant-system components and seals age out on a calendar, not an odometer, so a 47k-mile untouched example needs the same coolant pipes, hoses, air springs, tires and fluids as a 120k-mile one. Plan on $4,000–$8,000 of catch-up in the first year even on a clean, running example, and buy at a price that leaves that headroom.

profiles.label: Porsche Cayenne Turbo (957, 4.8L Twin-Turbo V8)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 957 Turbo is a cheap-to-buy, expensive-to-keep family hauler that happens to do 0-60 in 4.7 seconds and tow 7,700 lbs — a Monterey-Peninsula daily that can run Highway 1, haul dogs and bikes, and still handle a dirt road to a trailhead. The purchase price is now the smallest number in the ownership equation: a $20k car with $10k of deferred air suspension, PDCC, coolant, transfer case and brake work is a bad deal, while a $35k car with a documented $15k of that work already done is usually the cheaper car. Because the buyer wants documented and unmodified examples, lifted/light-barred/cat-deleted trucks are a poor fit — especially in California, where a 2008 gasoline Cayenne needs a biennial smog check and a change-of-ownership smog on initial registration. The right example is a two-owner, Porsche- or independent-specialist-serviced car with a thick folder, stock ride height, working air suspension and PDCC, and no overheating in its history.
profiles.weak_points:
1) Cooling system plumbing. The 4.8L (M48.50) fixed the notorious 4.5L plastic coolant pipes but replaced them with its own set of failure points: the plastic thermostat housing and coolant crossover/distribution pieces in the valley, the plastic-impeller water pump, and the rear coolant 'Y'. Typical failure window is 60k–100k miles or 10+ years; symptoms are sweet smell, low-coolant messages, and pink crust at the front of the valley or behind the alternator. Water pump + thermostat housing + hoses runs $1,800–3,500 with labor; a valley-pipe job or one done with the intake off can reach $4,000+. Look for a receipt naming water pump, thermostat housing, and coolant pipes — and confirm no head-gasket or overheat episode preceded it.

2) Crankcase ventilation (AOS/vent hoses). The molded crankcase vent hoses go brittle and collapse or split, causing rough idle, a whistle, oil consumption, and misfire/lean codes. Parts are cheap, labor is not: $600–1,500. Nearly every 100k-mile car needs this once.

3) Turbochargers and boost plumbing. Wastegate rattle, coked bearings after hot shutdowns, and cracked/leaking pressure pipes and diverter valves. A pair of factory turbos is $7,000–12,000 installed; rebuilds $4,000–6,000. Blue smoke on startup or after coasting, a shrill whine, or boost-deviation codes (P0299/P0234) are walk-away territory unless priced in. Ask for an oil-consumption figure per 1,000 miles and any boost-leak test results.

4) Direct injection carbon buildup. The 4.8L DFI V8 cokes its intake valves; by 80k–120k miles expect rough cold idle and misfires. Walnut blasting is $900–1,800. Coils and plugs are a routine 60k item ($600–1,200 for eight of each).

5) Air suspension. Rear air springs and front struts leak (car sits down overnight, 'Level control system fault'), the compressor burns out from chasing leaks, the valve block sticks, and ride-height sensors fail. OEM front strut $1,100–1,800 each, rear bag $500–900 each, compressor $700–1,400, all installed. A car that hasn't had at least a compressor and one or two corners done by 120k miles is due. Aftermarket lift kits and adjustable control arms fight the level-control calibration and wear ball joints/CV boots fast.

6) PDCC (Porsche Dynamic Chassis Control). Hydraulic active anti-roll bars — pump, lines, and bar actuators leak; a failed system throws a chassis warning and cannot be cheaply deleted. Repairs commonly land $2,500–6,000. If the listing mentions PDCC, demand evidence the system holds pressure and shows no faults.

7) Transfer case / AWD unit. The 957's transfer case chain stretches and the range/clutch actuator servo fails: symptoms are a grind or clunk on tight turns, 'Transfer case fault — 4WD limited,' or driveline shudder. Replacement transfer case is $3,500–6,000; this is the single most common big-dollar surprise on high-mile cars.

8) Driveshaft (cardan) center bearing and flex discs. Vibration at 40–70 mph or a shudder from a stop. Shaft replacement $1,200–2,500; some shops rebuild the center bearing for less.

9) Transmission (Aisin TR-60SN 6-speed). Durable if serviced, but Porsche called the fluid 'lifetime.' Neglected units show torque-converter shudder, 2-3 flare, or limp mode. Fluid, filter and pan service is $700–1,100; a rebuild/replacement is $5,000–8,000. Also common: the shifter/park-position (gear selector) switch failing to recognize Park — the example listing's exact complaint — a $400–900 fix but a tow-truck event when it strands you.

10) Secondary air injection. P0410/P0491-92 from a failed SAI pump or clogged passages; pump $600–1,200. A live smog-check concern in California.

11) Brakes. Turbo six-piston fronts with big rotors: a full four-corner pad-and-rotor job is $2,200–4,000 with OEM parts, and warped/lipped rotors are common on a car used as a mall SUV. Check for the rear electric parking-brake actuator and cable corrosion.

12) Emissions hardware. Secondary-cat bypass pipes, aftermarket downpipes, or missing cats mea
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up on almost any example: engine oil, transmission fluid/filter/pan gasket, transfer case fluid, front and rear diff fluid, brake fluid, coolant (~$1,500–2,500 total). Expect an air-suspension leak to surface within weeks (one strut/bag plus compressor, $1,200–2,500). Crankcase vent hoses and a vacuum-leak smoke test ($600–1,500). Coils/plugs and air filters if not receipted in the last 40k miles ($700–1,400). Tires — most of these cars wear staggered 265/50-19 or 275/45-20 and need a matched set of four for the AWD system ($1,400–2,200). Alignment after any suspension work. Fix any Park-position/shifter switch fault before it leaves you stranded. For a California-bound car: restore factory catalysts and stock ride height as needed to pass smog and referee, if the car has
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump, thermostat housing and accessible coolant pipes if not already documented ($1,800–3,500). Walnut-blast intake valves ($900–1,800). Brakes all around on a Turbo ($2,200–4,000). Remaining air-suspension corners and ride-height sensors ($1,500–3,000). Front control arm bushings, tie rods, and sway bar links ($1,200–2,500). Driveshaft center bearing or flex discs if any 40–70 mph vibration ($1,200–2,500). Serpentine belt, tensioner, pulleys, battery and battery-management reset. Budget the transfer case as a probable within-two-years item on anything past 120k miles ($3,500–6,000). Miscellaneous: sunroof drains, door latch actuator, tailgate struts, PCM/camera quirks.
profiles.market_notes: 957 Turbos have bottomed out and trade largely on records and mileage rather than spec: sub-80k-mile, single-dealer-serviced cars with air suspension and PDCC working bring $28k–45k, while 120k+ mile examples with thin history land in the high teens to mid-$20s — the example's $22,000 for a 137k-mile modified car is market-correct, not a bargain. Documentation of the expensive jobs (coolant/water pump, air struts, transfer case, turbos) is worth more than low mileage without paperwork. Turbo S and rare colors/interiors (Chestnut Brown or natural leather, Meteor Grey, GTS-style options) carry a small premium; black-on-black high-mile cars are the floor. Off-road builds, lift kits, light bars and cat bypasses actively reduce the pool of buyers and are a liability in California.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 15-plus-year-old 957 Turbo needs age-based work regardless of mileage: every rubber coolant and vacuum hose, the crankcase vent plumbing, plastic thermostat housing, air-spring bellows, control arm bushings, tires (date codes matter more than tread), battery and battery-management, and all drivetrain fluids. Budget $4,000–7,000 of catch-up in year one on a good example and treat the transfer case, air struts, and turbos as scheduled future expenses rather than surprises.

profiles.label: Porsche Cayman / Cayman S (987.2, DFI)
profiles.framing: The 987.2 is the sweet spot of the mid-engine Porsche line for a real-world driver: the 2009+ DFI engines (2.9 base, 3.4 S) shed the M96/M97 IMS bearing and bore-scoring anxiety that haunts the 987.1, and the chassis is still small, light, hydraulically steered, and immensely usable. For this buyer it is a Monterey Peninsula weekend and errand car that can also take Highway 1 or a canyon run without drama, and can absorb a real road trip with front and rear trunks. What matters most is documented maintenance from a Porsche specialist, an unmolested drivetrain and suspension, no track history, and a clean, complete car rather than the cheapest example. Options and transmission matter enormously to resale here — a well-optioned manual S in a real color is a different asset than a base-spec PDK.
profiles.weak_points: Water pump and thermostat: plastic impeller pumps are a consumable, typically 60k–90k miles or 8–10 years; symptoms are weeping from the pump vent hole, pink crust on the block, or slow warm-up. Budget $900–$1,600 installed; look for a receipt in the last ~60k. Coolant expansion tank and its cap crack with age — cheap parts, but a low-coolant light or crusty residue at the tank seam signals neglect. Radiators and A/C condensers sit low in the front bumper and pack with leaves and debris; corrosion-through causes coolant loss and the front radiator ducts trap moisture. Ask for photos of the front radiator area with the ducts removed and check for the debris-screen retrofit; a pair of radiators plus condensers is $1,800–$3,000. Rear main seal and AOS: the DFI engines are far better than 987.1 but still weep; a smoky cold-start plume or oil at the bellhousing means AOS ($700–$1,200) or RMS/clutch-out job ($2,000–$3,500 on a manual, more if the PDK must come out). Coil packs and DFI high-pressure fuel system: coil failure causes misfire codes and rough idle, cheap to fix; the high-pressure fuel pump and DFI injectors are the expensive tail — injector or HPFP work runs $1,200–$2,500. Carbon buildup on intake valves is inherent to direct injection; by 80k–100k expect mild hesitation and rough cold idle, walnut blasting $900–$1,500. PDK: the 7-speed dual-clutch is robust but requires fluid and filter service every ~40k miles at $700–$1,000; a neglected PDK with juddering low-speed engagement or delayed 1–2 shifts is a mechatronic/clutch-pack risk of $4,000–$9,000+. Demand a dated PDK service invoice, not a seller's recollection. Manual cars: dual-mass flywheel and clutch typically 60k–100k; a rattling clutch pedal at idle or high engagement point means $2,500–$3,500 with an RMS and IMS-free rear-end reseal. Suspension bushings and control arms: by 80k the rear toe links, front lower control arm bushings and top mounts are tired — squeaks over expansion joints, wandering alignment; a full round of arms and an alignment is $1,800–$3,500. Coilover conversions (Bilstein PSS9/PSS10) on an old car usually mean worn shock seals and a track past; PASM cars with a leaking OE damper are $1,000+ each. Rear decklid spoiler mechanism jams or throws a fault; motor/mechanism $600–$1,200. Ignition switch and the alarm/immobilizer module, plus the door-lock actuators and the microswitches in the doors, cause phantom drains and no-crank conditions; a parasitic draw complaint deserves investigation. Interior: soft-touch coating on the center console, glovebox and door pulls turns sticky with sun exposure; the Sport Chrono stopwatch bezel and the cupholder arms break. Bore scoring is largely a 987.1 issue but a borescope of all six cylinders and a leakdown are still the right money on any 15-year-old flat six. Finally, aftermarket high-flow cats: they routinely set P0420/P0430 and are not California-legal — a CEL from cats is a smog and registration problem in Carmel, not a cosmetic annoyance, and OE manifolds/cats to restore are $2,000–$4,000.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Fluids and filters if not documented within a year (engine oil, brake fluid on a 2-year cycle, coolant condition check). PDK fluid and filter service if there is no dated invoice within 40k miles. Full four-wheel alignment, especially on a coilover-equipped car. Tires: verify DOT dates — anything over 6 years old gets replaced regardless of tread, and mismatched front/rear brands (Michelin front, Continental rear as in the example) should be corrected to a matched staggered set, ~$1,400–$2,000. Brake pads and rotors if Hawk HP Plus track pads are fitted; those are unusable on the street (noise, cold bite) — swap to OE-spec pads and rotors, $1,200–$1,800. Diagnose and resolve any CEL: on a California-registered car, aftermarket cats setting P0420/P0430 must be addressed to pass smog, likely
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if not already replaced. Radiators and condensers if the front-end inspection shows corrosion or fin damage. Walnut-blast carbon cleaning and new spark plugs/coils at 90k–100k. Rear suspension bushings, toe links and drop links; front lower control arms if bushings are cracked. AOS if any cold-start smoke appears. Clutch and DMF on a manual approaching 90k. Serpentine belt, brake fluid flush, and a second oil service. Convertible-top items do not apply, but the rear spoiler mechanism and door-lock actuators are common one-off $600–$1,200 hits. Interior soft-touch trim refinishing if the sticky-coating problem is present.
profiles.market_notes: Manual transmission commands a meaningful premium over PDK on 987.2 Caymans and that gap has widened; PDK cars are the value play but sell slower. The S (3.4 DFI, 320 hp) is worth clearly more than the 2.9 base, and the Cayman R is a separate, much higher tier. Color and options drive the top of the market: PCCB-free but well-optioned cars in Guards Red, GT Silver, Aqua Blue, Peridot, or any PTS/special color with Sport Chrono, PASM, LSD, sport seats and full leather bring the money, while Arctic Silver over black is the most common and least differentiated combination. Documented Porsche-dealer or independent-specialist service history, a fresh PDK service, and a clean unmodified state are worth thousands; aftermarket cats, coilovers, harness bars and a CEL suggest track use and push a car firmly into the discount tier — realistically 15–25% under a stock, documented equivalent. Mileage bands matter less than records; 60k–90k with a binder beats 45k with a shrug.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 80k-mile 987.2 is now 15 years old and due for a full round of rubber and cooling: water pump/thermostat, coolant flush, expansion tank cap, radiator cleanout with debris screens, suspension bushings and toe links, and a fresh matched set of tires regardless of tread depth. DFI carbon cleaning and plugs land around 90k-100k. Plan roughly $4,000-$7,000 of catch-up in the first two years even on a well-kept car, and add the cost of restoring compliant catalytic converters if the car will be registered in California.

profiles.label: Saab 900 Turbo (Classic 900, 1979–1994)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the classic 900 Turbo is a charismatic, low-volume Swedish daily-driver — wraparound windshield, ignition on the console, a 16-valve B202 turbo with real mid-range shove, and a convertible body built by Valmet in Finland that is genuinely pleasant on Highway 1. It is not fast by modern standards and it is not a Porsche substitute; the appeal is the ergonomics, the torque curve, the airiness and the fact that almost none are left in honest, unmolested condition. The money question is never the purchase price, it is whether the car has been continuously maintained by someone who understood Saabs: oil-trap servicing, DI cassette, timing chain, and the transaxle-under-engine architecture that makes any clutch or chain job an engine-out event. Documented, stock, rust-free and cold-start-clean matters far more than mileage or a rare paint code.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Crankcase oil trap / PCV breather box (B202 turbo, effectively all mileages): the small mesh-and-baffle separator behind the intake clogs with sludge, pressurizes the crankcase and blows out the rear main, cam cover and dipstick seals, and in the worst case sludges the turbo feed. Cleaning is cheap ($100–300 with gaskets) if done every 30–50k; consequential damage is not. Look for receipts naming 'oil trap', 'breather box' or 'PCV service', and short (3–5k) synthetic oil intervals. 2) Turbocharger (Garrett T3, typically 100–160k): shaft play, oil seepage into the intake, smoke on spool-up, whistle changes. Rebuild/exchange $1,200–2,200 installed; wastegate actuator diaphragms also fail and cause overboost or lazy boost. 3) APC (Automatic Performance Control) boost/knock system: knock sensor, APC solenoid and the vacuum/boost hose web age out; symptoms are no boost, erratic gauge, or unrestrained overboost. Sensors/solenoids $150–400, hose sets cheap, diagnosis time-consuming. 4) Direct Ignition cassette (1988-on 16-valve): DI cassette and crank position sensor fail with age — misfire, no-start when hot, sudden stall. Genuine cassettes are $350–700 and getting scarce; a receipt within the last 10 years is a strong plus. 5) Timing chain, tensioner and guides (150k+ or any car with cold-start rattle): the single chain and plastic guides wear; a 2–5 second rattle at cold start is the tell. Job is $1,200–2,200 because of the tilted, transaxle-mounted engine layout. 6) Head gasket / cylinder head (120k+, worse on overheated or overboosted cars): coolant loss without external leak, white smoke, combustion pressure in the expansion tank. $1,800–3,000; add head skim/valve work. 7) Transaxle (the engine sits on top of the gearbox): 2nd-gear synchro crunch, differential/pinion whine, worn primary chain between crank and input shaft, and sloppy shift linkage bushings. Clutch replacement requires lifting the engine — $1,800–3,000 even when the clutch itself is a $400 part; assume the clutch is due if there is no receipt. 8) Oil leaks generally: rear main, sump gasket, cam cover, turbo oil return, and the power-steering rack/pump. Wet undersides are the norm; distinguish seep from streaming. 9) Convertible-specific: hydraulic top pump and rams leak (fluid in the trunk area, slow or one-sided operation), the top frame links and the header-rail/side seals harden and leak at the A-pillars, and the plastic rear window crazes. Frame/cylinder repair $800–2,500; a quality top installation is $2,000–4,000; original-pattern frame parts are scarce. Also check floor and footwell dampness from clogged cowl/plenum drains. 10) Rust: front subframe/crossmember and its mounting points, inner and outer sills and jacking points, floor pans, rear wheel arches, and — critically — the windshield surround under the wraparound glass, where a leaking screen rots the A-pillar base. Windshield-surround repair means glass out, $2,000–5,000+. 11) Cooling system: plastic-tank radiator, water pump, thermostat housing, hoses and heater control valve; heater core replacement is a dash-out job ($1,200–2,000). Any overheating history is a head-gasket flag. 12) Steering and front suspension: steering column lower U-joint and rack mounting bushings produce the classic 'play in the steering'; lower control arm bushings, upper strut mounts, sway-bar bushings and tie rods all wear in 60–80k cycles. A full front refresh is $1,200–2,500. 13) Electrical gremlins: bulb-failure sensor, ignition switch/steering lock in the console, power-window motors and regulators, headlight wiper motors, cornering-light and fog-light wiring, and dry/cracked engine-bay harness insulation. 14) Interior and trim: cracked dash top (often hidden by a molded dash cap — lift it and look), sagging headliner, broken seat-heater elements, brittle switch plastics, and pre-1993 A/C originally R12 — confirm whether it was properly converted to R134a (compressor, drier, hoses) or just topped off.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service including gearbox oil; remove and clean the crankcase oil trap/breather box and replace its gaskets; renew all vacuum/boost hoses and check APC function on a road test with the boost gauge; new plugs and (if undocumented) DI cassette; radiator/heater hose and belt inspection with replacement of anything 10+ years old; brake fluid flush plus inspection of rear calipers/flex lines; tighten up the steering column U-joint and rack bushings if the reported play persists after the 2026 work; clear the cowl and top-well drains, reseal or adjust the header rail and A-pillar seals, and service the convertible top hydraulics; alignment after any suspension work. Budget $1,500–3,000 at an independent Saab-literate shop.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and rear main seal if there is no receipt (engine-out, $2,000–3,000 combined and logically done together); front suspension bushings/struts/tie rods to remove the last of the vagueness; turbo inspection or exchange if shaft play or oil smoke appears; A/C compressor/drier and a proper R134a conversion if the system is weak; radiator and water pump on a 30+ year-old cooling system; exhaust from the downpipe back (original systems are long gone and aftermarket pieces fit poorly); convertible top frame links, side seals or a new top if the current one is aging; shift linkage bushings and a dash cap replaced with a proper repair if the underlying dash is cracked.
profiles.market_notes: Convertibles and SPG/Aero hatches carry a large premium over ordinary 900S cars; a 5-speed turbo is worth meaningfully more than an automatic, and automatics also suffer in the market for their fragility. Rare factory colors — Monte Carlo Yellow, Talladega Red, Edwardian Grey on an SPG — plus a documented window sticker, intact books and continuous service history can add 30–60% over a clean but anonymous example. Mileage matters less than evidence: a 130k car with oil-trap, DI, chain and top receipts routinely beats a 70k unknown, while Carfax accident entries, dash caps hiding cracks, non-original tops, aftermarket boost controllers or Hirsch/Abbott-style tuning without records all pull money out. Top of market for concours-level MCY convertibles has reached the mid-$20Ks–$30Ks; honest drivers sit $10,000–18,000.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 30-plus-year-old 900 needs a systematic rubber-and-seal catch-up: every vacuum/boost hose, coolant hose, fuel line, engine mount, suspension bushing and top seal is at or past end of life regardless of mileage. Plan $2,500–4,000 over the first two years just on age-related items, plus the engine-out clutch/rear-main job if no receipt exists, and source parts early through Saab specialists since classic 900 convertible and MCY-specific trim is drying up.

profiles.label: Subaru Forester 2.5 XT (SG, turbo)
profiles.framing: The SG Forester XT is the practical enthusiast answer to a WRX: same EJ255 turbo flat-four and AWD driveline in a tall, airy, cargo-friendly wagon with real ground clearance for Carmel-area fire roads and Sierra trips. For this buyer it is a do-everything daily that happens to run 13s, and the whole purchase decision hinges on one question: has this specific engine been detonated, over-boosted, or oil-starved by a previous owner. A documented, stock-tuned, well-maintained 5MT XT is a genuinely usable car; a mystery-tuned, big-turbo example is a short-block bill waiting to happen. Coastal California cars are a rust-exposure win, but salt-belt trade-ins circulate heavily in this model and must be inspected underneath before any price is agreed.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Ringland failure (EJ255, typically #4 piston) is the signature death of this engine — lean/knock events from aggressive or stale aftermarket tunes, cheap fuel, or a failing MAF/boost control. Symptoms: low compression on one cylinder, blow-by out the oil fill, puff of smoke at startup, rough idle. Cost: $5,000–8,000 for a quality short block install; expect leakdown/compression numbers as evidence before purchase. 2) Turbo (VF40) failure from oil-feed starvation: the banjo bolt at the turbo contains a fine filter screen that clogs with sludge and kills the bearing — Subaru issued the fix of replacing the bolt/screen and cleaning the oil pickup. Symptoms: whine, shaft play, blue smoke, boost drop. $1,500–2,500 installed; ask for receipts showing the banjo bolt/screen was addressed. 3) Head gasket weeping: turbo EJs use MLS gaskets so external coolant seepage is less common than in N/A 2.5s, but at 120k+ combustion-gas-into-coolant and oil seepage at the head-to-block joint do happen, often revealed by pressurized coolant, sweet smell, or a failed combustion-gas test — $2,200–3,200 with timing service bundled. 4) Timing belt, tensioner, idlers and water pump on a 105k-mile/8-year interval; a 2007 at 140k should show two services. Undocumented belt on an interference engine is a $1,200–1,600 immediate job or a catastrophic gamble. 5) Oil leaks: cam carrier/cam seals, valve cover gaskets (baked by turbo heat on the passenger side), front crank seal, and rear main seal — commonly $400–1,400 depending on how many are weeping and whether the timing cover is already coming off. 6) TGV (tumble generator valve) assemblies carbon up and stick, throwing P1152/P1153-type codes and rough running; delete plates or new assemblies $300–800. Related: PCV valve, clogged air/oil separator, and dirty MAF causing lean spikes. 7) Catalytic converter and knock-sensor codes: the factory pre-cat restricts and eventually crumbles (P0420), and the single knock sensor (P0325) is a cheap but critical part — cats $900–1,800, sensor $150–300. 8) Drivetrain: the 5MT (TY754) is the desirable spec but 2nd/3rd gear synchro wear, worn shifter bushings, and clutch life of 80–120k are normal; clutch with rear main seal $1,300–2,000. The 4EAT automatic with VTD is durable if fluid was changed but suffers torque-converter shudder and slow shifts, and a rebuild is $2,500–3,500. Mismatched-circumference tires destroy center differentials/transfer clutches — check all four tires for the same make, model and tread depth. 9) Rear wheel bearings (and front hubs) are a known wear item — growl that changes with load, $450–750 per corner. 10) Suspension age: front lower control arm bushings, rear trailing arm bushings, strut mounts, sway-bar end links and 20-year-old struts all together are a $1,200–2,500 refresh; sagging rear springs with cargo are typical. 11) Rust on non-California cars: rear wheel-arch lips, rocker seams behind the plastic cladding, rear subframe and lateral-link mounting points, strut tower tops, and the fuel-filler area. Perforation at subframe mounts is a structural walk-away. 12) Water intrusion: sunroof drain tubes clog and wet the headliner and A-pillars, rear hatch seals and the third brake light/hatch harness leak into the cargo area, and front quarter-window gussets leak onto the carpet — check for musty smell, stained headliner, and corroded rear-hatch wiring. 13) Electrical/interior wear: power window regulators, sunroof motor, failing dash cluster illumination, driver seat bolster and heated-seat elements, and a sagging headliner are all age-standard. 14) Modified examples: staged tunes, larger turbos, and E85 conversions are extremely common on this model and vastly increase risk — without a tuner's datalogs (knock/feedback correction, AFR), receipts for the fuel system, and an Accessport read of stored trouble codes, assume the engine is a lottery ticket.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service (oil with a quality filter, gearbox and front/rear diff fluid, coolant, brake fluid); replace all four tires with a matched set if there is any circumference mismatch; timing belt/water pump/tensioner/idler kit if not documented within 100k miles or 8 years; turbo oil-feed banjo bolt and oil pickup inspection/cleaning; new spark plugs and air filter; MAF cleaning; PCV valve; clear and re-read stored codes and knock data; address any active oil or coolant seep, sunroof drain cleanout, and worn sway-bar end links or strut mounts found on the test drive. Budget $1,800–3,500.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch and rear main seal if the pedal is high or the car has 100k+ on the original; valve cover and cam carrier gaskets; one or two wheel bearings; struts/springs and control arm bushings; catalytic converter or O2 sensor for a P0420; radiator (plastic end tanks) and thermostat; front brake rotors/pads; battery, alternator or AC compressor as age items; possible TGV cleaning or delete and a return-to-stock or professionally re-verified tune. Budget $2,500–4,500.
profiles.market_notes: The 5MT XT Limited is the spec that moves money; automatics trade meaningfully cheaper and are harder to resell to enthusiasts. Documented timing-belt and head-gasket history, a stock or reputably tuned engine, and clean underbody (West Coast car) are worth more than low miles on a mystery car. WR Blue, Aspen White and the rarer 2008 Sports XT trim draw crowds, and heavily built JDM-STi-style cars occasionally clear $25k+ on auction sites — but that is enthusiast-auction money, not a floor for a driver-grade example, which is typically a $8k–16k car at 100–160k miles.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2007 XT is a 18-plus-year-old, 130k–160k-mile turbo car, so assume a deferred-maintenance catch-up round: timing belt kit and water pump, all fluids including diffs, plugs, PCV, coolant hoses and radiator, struts and bushings, one or two wheel bearings, and re-sealing the usual cam carrier and valve cover oil seeps. Plan $3,000–5,000 over the first year on top of purchase price even for a clean, documented example, and keep the short-block reserve intact until compression numbers prove the engine.

Dated receipt for timing belt, water pump, tensioner and idlers

profiles.label: Sunbeam Tiger Mk 1 / Mk 1A (260 V8)
profiles.framing: A Tiger is a small, light, honestly crude British roadster with a Ford small-block shoehorned into it by Shelby's shop and built by Rootes on a shoestring. For a Carmel-based owner it is a Sunday-morning Highway 1 and Laguna Seca paddock car: short-hop fun, big torque, terrible ergonomics, and genuine period charisma; it is not a road-trip car and it is not a commuter. What matters most is authenticity (Alpine-to-Tiger 'Algers' are everywhere), the structural condition of a unibody that was never engineered for 200+ lb-ft, and whether the cooling/heat-soak issues have been solved properly. A documented, TAC-authenticated car with sorted brakes, cooling and wiring is worth paying a lot more for than a shiny one with no paper.
profiles.weak_points: 1) AUTHENTICITY FIRST. Roughly a third of 'Tigers' offered for sale are converted Alpines or re-bodied/re-stamped cars. Mk 1 LHD chassis numbers run B9470001-onward (Mk 1A B9471... series), with the serial plate on the left inner fender/engine bay and a separate JAL (Jensen assembly) number; body stamps, the Panhard rod mount, the rack delete and the Burman steering box mount are all conversion tells. Absence of a Tiger Authentication Committee (TAC) certificate or a Norman Miller build-details letter is a 20-40% value haircut, and on a car with weld-in structure or fresh paint over the stampings it's a walk-away. 2) RUST, and it hides. Check the front frame rails/crossmember ahead of the radiator, inner and outer sills/rockers, floor pans under both seats, footwell toe boards, the battery area, rear spring hangers and their body-mount boxes, trunk floor and spare well, rear wheel arches and doglegs. Rootes rustproofing was nil and these live in coastal California with salt-air and top-down parking. Proper sill/floor/spring-hanger repair is $12k-35k with paint; a full body-off restoration is $80k-150k+ and will never be recovered on a Mk 1. 3) STRUCTURAL FATIGUE from V8 torque: cracking around the rear leaf-spring front hangers, Panhard rod anchor, differential snubber, and the transmission tunnel/crossmember. Look for stress cracks, added plating, and doors that won't shut squarely when the car is jacked at one corner. 4) OVERHEATING AND HEAT SOAK is the defining Tiger complaint. Stock radiator and packaging leave almost no airflow; expect 210-230F in traffic, vapor lock, a cooked footwell and a steering column that runs beside the exhaust. Sorted cars have an aluminum radiator, shroud and electric fan, header wrap or ceramic coating, insulation, and a phenolic carb spacer - budget $1,500-3,000 to do this properly if it hasn't been done. 5) STEERING: the Tiger uses a Burman worm-and-roller box (the Alpine's rack wouldn't clear the V8) with a fragile, heat-soaked column and a rag joint. Play, wander and column lash are endemic; a rebuilt box or a modern R&P conversion runs $1,200-3,500. 6) CLUTCH SLAVE/HYDRAULICS are packaged so badly that the classic Tiger job is 'pull the engine to change the slave cylinder' unless a remote or through-the-hole kit is fitted; a $60 part becomes a $1,200-2,000 job. Ask when the clutch, slave and master were last done. 7) OIL FILTER CLEARANCE: no room for a spin-on filter against the steering box, so a remote filter/adapter is near-mandatory; badly done remote lines are a known fire/oil-starvation risk - inspect hose routing and age. 8) ENGINE: almost no Tiger retains its original 260 (5-bolt bellhousing, correct block casting and engine number on the STOA/TAC paperwork). 289s and 302s are extremely common and are not a defect in a driver, but they cost real money at the top of the market. On any small-block, check for oil pressure at hot idle, rear main seepage, and whether the 289/302 firing-order camshaft issue was addressed with the correct distributor/cam combination. Rebuilds run $8k-15k. 9) DRIVELINE: the BorgWarner T-10 four-speed has weak 2nd-gear synchro and whines; rebuild $1,800-3,000, 5-speed (Tremec TKO/T5) conversions are common and improve drivability but cost originality points. Rear axle is a Salisbury 4HU (Mk 1/1A) - listen for whine and check for pinion-seal leaks and Panhard rod bushing slop. 10) BRAKES: Girling front discs/rear drums with a vacuum servo that routinely fails; steel lines corrode, and the Tiger is genuinely underbraked for its power. Full hydraulic refresh $1,500-3,000; Wilwood conversions are the usual fix. 11) FUEL SYSTEM: twin rear-fender tanks joined by a crossover hose and vent lines that rot out of sight and dump fuel into the trunk area. Old tanks, sending units and rubber are a fire risk - replacement/lining $800-2,500. Also watch for ethanol-rotted pump diaphragms and hard fuel lines routed near headers. 12) LUCAS ELECTRICS AND WIRING: 60-year-old h
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid and hose service including the fuel crossover and vent hoses; brake hydraulic inspection with likely master/slave/wheel cylinder and flex-hose replacement; cooling system verification under a 20-minute hot idle with an IR thermometer, plus fan/shroud fixes if it climbs; carburetor tune and ignition timing/dwell set with correct distributor curve; battery, grounds and charging check; steering box adjustment or rebuild and rag-joint replacement; tire date codes - almost every Tiger on the market wears 8-12 year-old rubber that must be replaced regardless of tread; wheel alignment and rear Panhard/spring bushing check. Budget $2,500-5,000.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Clutch hydraulics with a remote-slave fix if not already done; T-10 synchro rebuild or accept a 5-speed; leaf springs, bushings and shocks; fuel tank cleaning/lining and new sender; exhaust/header heat management and footwell insulation; gauge and switch rebuilds and likely partial rewiring; convertible top and windshield/door seals; localized rust repair at sills, spring hangers or trunk floor discovered after purchase; differential pinion seal and axle service. Budget $5,000-12,000 depending on what the PPI finds.
profiles.market_notes: Mk 2 cars (289, 633 built, distinctive egg-crate grille) trade at roughly double a comparable Mk 1; within Mk 1/1A, TAC authentication plus documented original-type engine, a factory hardtop, and known ownership history are the biggest value levers. Correct or period colors and LAT/Shelby-era dealer options add; modified restomods - 302s, coilovers, 5-speeds, Wilwoods, non-stock wheels - drive beautifully and sell to a narrower audience, typically well under concours-original money regardless of how much was spent. Driver-quality authenticated Mk 1s generally sit in the $45k-75k band, strong restored cars $85k-130k, with no-paperwork or suspected-Alger cars much lower and hard to resell. Receipts matter more than mileage on a 60-year-old five-digit odometer.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 60-year-old car is due for everything rubber and hydraulic regardless of presentation: fuel crossover and vent hoses, brake and clutch hydraulics, coolant hoses, suspension bushings, top seals and tires by date code. Even a $200k-receipts show car needs a shakedown-and-sort budget because low post-restoration mileage means untested systems, and a Tiger's two chronic subsystems - cooling and wiring - are the ones that strand or burn cars.

profiles.label: Toyota 4Runner N210 (4th Gen, 2003–2009)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the N210 is a 20-year-old body-on-frame family/adventure rig that should still be a low-drama daily driver: Highway 1 commuting, Big Sur trailheads, dump runs, and the occasional Sierra snow trip. The value proposition is Toyota durability plus real 4WD hardware, so the entire decision hinges on whether THIS truck has been kept out of salt and given honest fluid service — not on trim badges. A documented, unmodified, rust-free Western or Southern-dry example at 100–180k miles is a better buy than a low-mileage Rust Belt truck at any price. Automatic is the only transmission offered and is completely normal here.
profiles.weak_points: 1) FRAME AND UNDERBODY RUST is the single generation-defining risk. Midwest/Northeast trucks rot at the rear frame rails above the axle, the rear spring/shackle hangers, the crossmember behind the transfer case, and the body mounts. Toyota's frame rust campaigns largely covered Tacoma/Tundra/Sequoia, not the 4Runner, so there is no warranty backstop. Fresh black undercoating or 'fresh paint' on the underside of an auction truck from a salt state is a red flag, not a feature — it hides scale. A rotten frame is a walk-away, not a repair. 2) 'PINK MILKSHAKE' — on 2003–2005 (and some 2006) trucks the transmission cooler lives inside the radiator; when the internal barrier fails, coolant enters the ATF and destroys the A750F 5-speed. Symptoms: pink/strawberry-milkshake ATF on the dipstick, low coolant, harsh or slipping shifts. Prevention is a radiator replacement with an external cooler ($600–1,000); the cure after contamination is a transmission ($3,500–5,500 installed). Look for a radiator replacement receipt or verify clean red ATF and clean coolant. 3) REAR AIR SUSPENSION / X-REAS. Limited models (and some V8s) used a rear height-control air system whose bags, compressor and height sensors fail; Sport Edition used X-REAS cross-linked dampers with a center transfer valve. Both are expensive ($1,200–2,500 for OEM parts) and are commonly 'fixed' by converting to conventional coilovers/shocks — a conversion is acceptable but must be documented. Sagging rear, compressor running constantly, or a bouncy/uneven ride are tells. 4) LOWER BALL JOINTS. 2003–2007 front lower ball joints are a known wear/failure item, especially with lifts or aftermarket parts; a failure drops a corner. Check for grease boot tears, clunks over bumps, and insist on Toyota/OEM-quality parts in any receipt ($400–900/side installed). 5) DASHBOARD CRACKING/STICKINESS. Very common on N210 in sun-belt cars; Toyota's extended coverage has expired. Full dash replacement runs $1,200–2,500; a cap is $250–500. Cosmetic but it moves price. 6) 1GR-FE V6 OIL SEEPAGE at the cam towers, timing cover, and front main. A weep is typical by 150k; an actual reseal means pulling the timing cover, $2,000–4,000. Look for oil film on the front of the block and drips on the skid plate. Head gaskets are NOT a chronic 1GR failure — if coolant loss is present, suspect radiator/heater lines first, but a block test is cheap insurance on any truck with unexplained coolant use. 7) 2UZ-FE V8 TIMING BELT + water pump every 90k miles / ~9 years, $900–1,600. It's a non-interference engine so a break usually won't bend valves, but a dead water pump will cook it. No belt receipt on a V8 = assume you're buying one. 8) ABS/VSC BRAKE ACTUATOR. The ABS pump/actuator assembly fails with ABS+VSC+TRAC lights and sometimes a buzzing pump; new OEM assemblies run $1,500–2,500, rebuilt units $500–900. Verify all warning lamps extinguish after start. 9) POWER REAR WINDOW (tailgate glass). The regulator/motor and its wiring harness in the hatch fail, and a leaking tailgate seal rots the lower tailgate and the rear sill from the inside. Cycle the glass up and down from both the key and the dash switch; pull the cargo mat and look for standing water. 10) REAR HATCH/QUARTER AND WHEEL-ARCH ROT even on otherwise clean trucks — check behind the rear wheels, the rocker pinch welds, and under the rear bumper cover. 11) FRONT DIFFERENTIAL ACTUATOR (ADD) on part-time 4WD trucks leaks and sticks; full-time 4WD/locking-center-diff trucks use a Torsen center diff whose locker actuator can also fail. Any 4WD system must be range-shifted 2WD-4HI-4LO and, if equipped, center-diff-locked on a test drive. 12) EXHAUST/SECONDARY ITEMS OF AGE: cracked exhaust manifold studs on high-mile V6s, tired original struts (fronts commonly leak by 120k, $800–1,400 for a full set installed), steering rack and pump seeps, brittle radiator/heater hoses, and a heater blower resistor/AC amplifier that kills fan speeds. 13) HIGH-MILE V6 WATER PU
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service if records are thin: engine oil, ATF drain-and-fill (Toyota WS, no aggressive flush), front/rear diff and transfer case gear oil, coolant (Toyota SLLC), brake fluid. Replace the radiator with an external trans cooler on any 2003–2006 without a radiator receipt. Four tires if date codes are over 6 years old regardless of tread, plus an alignment. New wiper blades, cabin/engine air filters, and likely a battery. Expect a rear tailgate glass seal or regulator fix, a dash cap or trim tidy, and correcting any minor oil/coolant seep. Budget $1,500–3,000.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Struts/shocks all around if not recently done ($800–1,400), lower ball joints and possibly upper control arm bushings, front brake pads/rotors, serpentine belt and idler/tensioner, water pump and thermostat on a V6 over 130k, timing belt/water pump on any V8 without documentation ($900–1,600), front cam-tower or timing-cover seepage monitoring, wheel bearings/hub if there's a growl, and exhaust hardware. If it's a Limited or Sport with air suspension or X-REAS still fitted, budget for a documented conventional conversion ($1,000–1,800). $2,000–4,000 typical.
profiles.market_notes: Rust-free provenance is worth more than mileage on this generation — a 160k California/Arizona truck with clean frame photos regularly beats a 65k Illinois truck. V6 (1GR-FE) commands a premium over the V8 for most buyers because of the timing chain and better fuel economy, though V8 fans like the smoothness; the V8/Limited's rear air suspension is a price drag unless converted. Desirable spec: 4x4 with the locking center differential (full-time 4WD), rear locker on Trail/Sport trucks, cloth over cracked leather, sunroof, and no third-row (rare and space-eating anyway). Unmodified, one/two-owner cars with a real service file and 2009 facelift trucks sit at the top; lifted, big-tire, light-bar builds and any pink-fluid transmission history sit at the bottom.
profiles.catchup_notes: Treat any N210 as needing a full 20-year fluid and rubber reset: all gear oils, ATF drain-and-fill with Toyota WS, coolant, brake fluid, hoses, belt, and tires by date code rather than tread. Even a 64k-mile example will have hardened bushings, aged struts, dried tailgate/door seals, and an original radiator that is living on borrowed time. Budget roughly $2,000–3,500 in the first year for catch-up work on an otherwise sound, rust-free truck.

profiles.label: Toyota Altezza / Lexus IS (XE10)
profiles.framing: This is a cheap, rear-drive, six-cylinder manual sedan bought to be driven on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road, not stored. The JDM AS200 with the J160 six-speed and an LSD is the interesting spec: 158hp of 1G-FE BEAMS inline-six that needs revs, in a light, well-balanced chassis with double-wishbone rear suspension. Because it is a fresh direct import with a Japanese service history that mostly does not translate, the real questions are body/underbody corrosion from Japanese winters, whether the timing belt has actually been done in the last decade, whether the J160 and clutch are healthy, and whether it can be legally titled and registered in California. Parts for JDM-only pieces (bumpers, lenses, RHD-specific trim, 1G-FE BEAMS ancillaries) are a mail-order-from-Japan exercise, so a car that is already complete and undamaged is worth far more than the bid gap suggests.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing belt on the 1G-FE BEAMS: rubber belt with hydraulic tensioner, nominal 100k km interval and an age limit of roughly 7-10 years regardless of distance. The sticker on this car claims service at 76k km — that is ~107k km and likely 15+ years ago. It is a non-interference-ish design in theory but the VVT-i cam gear and tensioner are the expensive parts; budget $900-1,500 for belt, tensioner, idlers, water pump, cam and crank seals, and the drive belts. Treat any car without a dated receipt as needing the job immediately. 2) VVT-i intake cam actuator: cold-start rattle/diesel-like clatter for 1-3 seconds is the classic symptom; also oil-fed, so it tolerates neglected oil poorly. Actuator ~$350-700 plus labor, usually bundled with the timing belt job. 3) Oil consumption and rear main / valve cover / cam-plug leaks: 1G-FE BEAMS at 150k+ km often uses 0.5-1qt per 1,000-1,500 miles via valve stem seals and PCV. Check the PCV valve and look for oil misting at the back of the head and the oil pan rail. Valve cover gasket $250-450; rear main with trans out $900-1,400. 4) J160 six-speed: the known weak spots are 2nd (and sometimes 3rd) synchro balk on fast cold shifts, input shaft/front bearing whine in neutral with clutch out, and a notchy 5th-6th shift when the oil is old. Toyota specified a specific 75W-90 GL-4; wrong fluid accelerates synchro wear. Rebuild or used-unit swap $1,800-3,500; a fluid change is the cheap first move. 5) Clutch hydraulics and clutch: master and slave cylinders leak with age (pedal goes soft/low engagement point creeps down), $200-450 for both. Clutch and rear main together $1,300-2,000 since the box is already out. 6) Rust from Japanese road salt: inspect rear wheel arch lips, the sills below the jacking points, the rear subframe and its mounting cradle, rear shock towers, the spare wheel well, the fuel and brake hard lines over the rear axle, and the exhaust hangers. Northern-Japan auction cars can be badly scaled underneath even with flawless paint. Any structural rear subframe or floor rot makes the car a parts donor at this price level. 7) Suspension bushings and rear geometry: at 180k km the rear upper/lower arm bushings, rear subframe bushings, front lower control arm bushings and sway bar links are typically done, producing clunks over expansion joints and a wandering rear under braking. Full bushing/shock refresh $1,600-2,800 with alignment; many components are shared with US IS300 so parts are obtainable. 8) Chronograph gauge cluster: dimming/dead cluster illumination, sticking or lazy needles, and dead LCD odometer segments are common; clusters are km-only and 180 km/h, and Japanese repair/refurb or a swap is the fix ($200-600). Verify the odometer against the auction sheet — Japanese odometer rollback exists though the Car VX/auction sheet usually catches it. 9) Climate control blend-door and servo actuators: clicking behind the dash, one-temperature-only output, and dead auto mode are typical; actuators $120-300 each plus dash disassembly. Also check the A/C — R134a systems of this age commonly need a compressor, drier and expansion valve, $900-1,600. 10) Ignition and sensors: coil-on-plug packs, crank/cam position sensors, knock sensor and the MAF drift with age and cause rough idle, hunting idle, or a P0335/P0325 code. An IACV/throttle body clean fixes most idle hunting; individual sensors $100-300 each. 11) Cooling system: original plastic-tank radiator, thermostat housing and the small hoses under the intake fail with age; a 25-year-old radiator on a tightly packaged inline-six should just be replaced ($400-700 with hoses and coolant). 12) Sunroof drains and interior water: clogged drains rot the front footwell carpet and short the under-carpet harness; check for damp padding and rust bubbles under the door sills. Power-folding mirror motors also fail ($150-300 per side). 13) JDM-specific legal and hardware items: 180 km/h speedometer and km odometer, JDM headlight beam pattern aimed
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full timing belt service with water pump, tensioner, idlers and front seals unless a dated receipt exists; complete fluid service (engine oil, J160 gear oil with correct GL-4 75W-90, LSD/diff oil, brake fluid, coolant); replace the cracked left-rear taillight lens and reseal to stop trunk water intrusion; new plugs, PCV valve, air filter and a throttle body/IACV clean; inspect and likely replace clutch master and slave cylinders; four tires if the Potenzas are date-coded older than ~6 years regardless of tread; headlight aim correction or US-pattern/left-traffic conversion for legality and for unlit Carmel Valley roads; CA DMV VIN verification plus BAR referee appointment and whatever it demands; wheel alignment; deal with any surface rust with a wash-down and underbody treatment before it
profiles.repairs_12mo: Radiator, hoses and thermostat; front and rear suspension bushings, shocks and sway bar links with alignment; clutch and rear main seal if the pedal or oil leak dictates; A/C service or compressor/drier if it blows warm; valve cover gasket and cam plug reseal; blend-door actuator(s) and cluster illumination repair; front lower ball joints and outer tie rods; exhaust hangers, rear brake calipers or rebuild kits if the rears are seized from sitting; possible J160 2nd-gear synchro work if it balks when hot; sorting or removal of the aftermarket Blaupunkt head unit wiring.
profiles.market_notes: XE10 values are driven by drivetrain and rust, not cosmetics: RS200 (3S-GE BEAMS, 210hp, six-speed, Torsen) commands a clear premium over AS200, and AS200 manual over AS200 automatic; the AS300/IS300 2JZ-GE cars sit in their own market. Fresh direct imports with a clean auction sheet, a documented timing belt, and a clean rust-free underbody sell well above generic $3-6k import money, while salt-belt Japanese cars with arch or subframe rot are effectively parts cars. Low km, unmodified interiors, working chronograph clusters, factory wheels and intact JDM lenses/bumpers add real dollars; big aftermarket wheels, non-original head units and cut-in exhausts subtract. Titling status matters — a car already on a clean US state title with import paperwork in hand is worth meaningfully more than one still in customs limbo, and a California buyer should discount for referee/registration risk.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 25-year-old Japanese-market car has had almost no preventive maintenance since its last shaken and that every rubber and plastic part is original: belts, hoses, radiator, bushings, motor/trans mounts, brake and clutch hydraulics, and all fluids. Budget a deliberate $3,000-4,500 catch-up program in the first year on top of the purchase price, plus time and shipping for JDM-only parts sourced from Japan.

profiles.label: Toyota Land Cruiser 200-Series (URJ200, 5.7L 3UR-FE)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the 200-series is a lifetime-grade family/adventure truck: full-time 4WD, locking center diff, CRAWL control, 8,100 lb tow rating, and a 3UR-FE V8 that routinely sees 300k miles with fluids and attention. It is not a value play — it is a buy-once vehicle where the purchase price is often the smallest number in the first three years, so documented maintenance and a clean, unbypassed emissions system matter more than mileage. The 2008-2011 cars (pre-facelift, DVD nav, no Entune) are the cheap entry point but carry the generation's two most expensive known faults. In California, the smog transfer requirement makes emissions-system honesty a purchase gate, not a nice-to-have.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Secondary air injection system (2008-2011 especially): the AIS pumps, switching valves and air-injection driver fail from moisture ingestion, throwing P2440/P2442/P0418/P1441-family codes and a CEL that appears on cold starts. Toyota's ZE4 warranty enhancement (10yr/150k) has expired on a 2008. Dealer repair with both pumps and valves runs $3,000-4,500; independent with quality aftermarket parts $1,800-3,000. Bypass/delete kits and ECU tricks will fail a California smog inspection or leave incomplete readiness monitors — ask specifically whether the system is intact. 2) Cam tower / timing cover oil leaks on the 3UR-FE: Toyota reseals the cam towers under TSB; symptoms are oil weeping down the rear of the heads, oil in the valley, and drips onto the bellhousing/exhaust (burnt oil smell). Because the intake, timing cover and often the heads come off, expect $3,500-6,500. Very common at 120k-200k. 3) Starter motor lives under the intake manifold; when it fails (typically 150k-220k) it is a 6-10 hour job, $1,200-2,000. Smart owners do it preemptively with the water pump or air-pump work — look for that receipt. 4) Water pump and thermostat: whining/weeping around 100k-150k, $900-1,400 done properly with coolant and belt. 5) KDSS (Kinetic Dynamic Suspension System): hydraulic sway-bar system with cylinders and a valve body on the driver's frame rail. Look for oil film on the cylinders/lines and for the truck sitting cocked or with one front corner high; seized valves or a leaking accumulator is $1,200-2,500 and must be bled correctly. 6) Front suspension wear: upper control arm ball joints (integral, arm replaced, ~$500-800/side), lower ball joints, sway bar end links and bushings, and leaking front shocks/struts — the listed 'small leak from the front left shock' is textbook and means a pair at minimum ($600-1,400 for quality OE-spec or Bilstein/OME). 7) Brakes: the 200 is 5,800 lbs and eats pads and rotors; full four-corner pads and rotors $800-1,400. The ABS/VSC brake actuator (skid-control ECU/pump) is a known high-cost failure — a flashing VSC/ABS/brake light cluster can mean $2,000-3,500. 8) Drivetrain fluids: Toyota calls the AB60F six-speed 'lifetime' WS fluid; at 185k with no records assume a drain-and-fill service ($250-400) and budget for the possibility of a tired torque converter. Transfer case, front and rear diffs should be on a 30k cycle — no records means do all three now ($300-450). 9) Exhaust manifold/header cracks and broken manifold studs cause a cold-start tick and can mimic an air-injection code; repair $800-2,000. 10) Radiator end tanks and the intercooler-free cooling stack: plastic tank seepage and a clogged radiator around 150k+, $700-1,100. 11) Drive shaft: non-greaseable U-joints and center support bearings produce a driveline shudder at 40-60 mph; replacement shaft or rebuild $500-1,200. 12) Electronics of the 2008-2011 era: DVD-based navigation and Bluetooth are obsolete, rear-seat entertainment screens fail, the rear hatch struts sag, and the rear A/C evaporator can leak — none are fatal, but a head-unit swap is $500-1,500. 13) Frame and body rust: California cars are usually fine, but many 200s migrate from the Rockies/Midwest — inspect frame rails behind the rear wheels, the KDSS lines, brake lines and the rear crossmember. 14) Modification risk: lifted, re-geared, big-tire or 'delete' trucks are common in this platform; a lift without an OEM-correct KDSS-compatible setup causes driveline vibration and premature CV/ball joint wear.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Front shocks/struts in pairs and sway bar end links and bushings ($900-1,800 for the front end done properly); brake pads and likely rotors all around ($800-1,400); full fluid catch-up — engine oil, transmission drain-and-fill, transfer case, front and rear differentials, brake fluid flush, coolant if not documented ($700-1,100); new tires if the set is over 6 years old or mismatched ($1,200-1,700 in 285/60R18); serpentine belt, PCV valve, engine and cabin air filters, and iridium plugs if not done by 120k ($500-900 with plugs); alignment after suspension work ($150-250). If any CEL or incomplete readiness monitor exists, resolving it to pass California smog before or immediately after purchase.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump/thermostat if not documented ($900-1,400); preemptive starter replacement done concurrently with any intake-off work ($1,200-2,000 standalone, far less as an add-on); secondary air injection pumps and valves if the system is original and untouched at this age ($1,800-3,500); upper control arms/ball joints ($1,000-1,600 the pair); cam tower reseal if any weep is developing ($3,500-6,500); radiator ($700-1,100); rear hatch struts, cabin blower resistor, and assorted 15-year-old rubber — bushings, hoses, hatch and door seals ($400-900); driveline center support bearing or U-joints if a shudder appears ($500-1,200).
profiles.market_notes: There is one US trim, so price moves on mileage bands, records, rust history, and whether the air-injection and cam-tower jobs are already done with receipts — a documented sub-150k California truck with those two items addressed commands a real premium over an undocumented 185k example. 2008-2011 cars are the value tier; the 2013+ facelift and especially 2016+ (8-speed, Safety Sense, Entune) step up several thousand dollars. Neutral colors with tan or grey leather and unmolested stock suspension sell fastest to this buyer type; big lifts, aftermarket bumpers and light bars narrow the buyer pool and add hidden wear. At 185k a clean, documented example in Northern California realistically trades in the low-to-mid $20s, so anything near $26k needs receipts, not just a seller's summary of a PPI.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 15-year-old, 185k-mile 200-series should be assumed to need a full fluid reset (transmission, transfer case, both diffs, coolant, brake fluid), a front-end refresh of shocks, links and bushings, and new tires — roughly $3,000-4,500 before touching the two headline jobs. The secondary air injection system and the cam tower reseal are the budget-defining unknowns: if neither has receipts, plan for one or both within two years. Everything else on this truck is ordinary Toyota wear that rewards preemptive work, especially bundling the starter with any intake-off service.
